# MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED ATTORNEY REVIEW. NOT LEGAL ADVICE.

**Jurisdiction:** United Kingdom. Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), Part 14 (Control of political donations and expenditure), section 378. The section is expressed to extend to the whole of the United Kingdom (the section heading carries the marginal extent marker "U.K.", i.e. England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland). *Companies Act 2006*, s. 378, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2014-06-13.

**Question presented:** In the text of section 378 stated to be up to date through 20 November 2026, what donation ceiling and what measuring period does the section state?

---

## 1. Answer in short

| Element | Answer |
|---|---|
| **Donation ceiling** | **£5,000** |
| **Measuring period** | **The period of 12 months ending with the date on which the donation in question is made** — a rolling backward-looking 12-month window, recalculated on the date of each donation. It is *not* the company's accounting period, *not* the financial year, and *not* a fixed calendar period. |
| **Dimension of the ceiling** | A **single aggregate pot**, not per party, not per candidate, not per recipient. The £5,000 covers the donation in question *plus* all "other relevant donations" (including those of subsidiaries / holding company / fellow subsidiaries as applicable) in that rolling 12 months, whoever the recipient. |
| **Effect** | Authorisation under Part 14 is not needed **except to the extent that** the aggregate exceeds £5,000. Only the excess requires authorisation. |

---

## 2. The provision, verbatim

**Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), section 378 — "Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month period"** (text as at 13 June 2014, which is the operative text through 20 November 2026 — see §3):

> **378 Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month period U.K.**
>
> (1) Authorisation under this Part is not needed for a donation except to the extent that the total amount of—
> (a) that donation, and
> (b) other relevant donations made in the period of 12 months ending with the date on which that donation is made,
> exceeds £5,000.
>
> (2) In this section—
> "donation" means a donation to a political party or other political organisation or to an independent election candidate; and
> "other relevant donations" means—
> (a) in relation to a donation made by a company that is not a subsidiary, any other donations made by that company or by any of its subsidiaries;
> (b) in relation to a donation made by a company that is a subsidiary, any other donations made by that company, by any holding company of that company or by any other subsidiary of any such holding company.
>
> (3) If or to the extent that a donation is exempt by virtue of this section from the requirement of authorisation under this Part, it shall be disregarded in determining what donations are authorised by any resolution passed for the purposes of this Part.

*Source: Companies Act 2006, s. 378, point-in-time view as at 13 June 2014, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2014-06-13 (text reproduced identically at https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/part/14/2026-04-06).*

---

## 3. Currency of the text through 20 November 2026 — verification

1. **Editorial currency statement.** legislation.gov.uk states on the section page: "Companies Act 2006, Section 378 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before **22 November 2026**." Because 22 November 2026 is later than 20 November 2026, the revised text covers the requested date. *Companies Act 2006*, s. 378, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2014-06-13; the same statement appears on Part 14 at https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/part/14/2026-04-06.
2. **No amendment since 13 June 2014.** The "Alternative versions" list for section 378 shows only two point-in-time versions: **01/10/2007** (Amendment) and **13/06/2014**. There is no version between 13 June 2014 and 22 November 2026, which indicates no amendment to section 378 has come into force in that interval. *Ibid.* (section page, "Changes over time for: Section 378" box).
3. **Textual identity across versions.** The operative words (£5,000; "the period of 12 months ending with the date on which that donation is made") are reproduced without variation in every version examined: 13/06/2014 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2014-06-13); the 26/05/2015 snippet view (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2015-05-26/data.xht?view=snippet); the 01/04/2025 point-in-time view (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/cy/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2025-04-01); and Part 14 as at 06/04/2026 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/part/14/2026-04-06).
4. **Residual caveat — record it in the file.** The same banner carries the standard warning: "There are changes that may be brought into force at a future date." No such change is listed against section 378, and none would be in force on 20 November 2026 on the material reviewed; but the banner is a statement about changes *known* to the editorial team, not a warranty. Before the figure is relied on in a live transaction, re-check the "Latest available (revised)" view and the "Changes to Legislation" area on the day of reliance.

**Conclusion on ask 2:** the version of section 378 in force on 20 November 2026 is the text as amended with effect from 13 June 2014, and it states a ceiling of £5,000 measured over the 12 months ending with the date of the donation.

---

## 4. How the ceiling and period operate — analysis

**4.1 Only the excess needs authorisation.** Section 378(1) disapplies the Part 14 authorisation requirement "except to the extent that" the aggregate exceeds £5,000. The first £5,000 of aggregate donations in any rolling 12-month window is exempt; the balance above £5,000 is not. The exemption is partial, not all-or-nothing. *Companies Act 2006*, s. 378(1), https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2014-06-13.

**4.2 The period is a rolling look-back, not an accounting period.** The measuring period is "the period of 12 months **ending with the date on which that donation is made**". *Ibid.*, s. 378(1)(b). Consequences the company secretary should note:
- There is no fixed window that resets on an accounting reference date. Each donation is tested against its own trailing 12 months.
- Two donations 12 months and one day apart do not aggregate; two donations 11 months apart do.
- A donation made on, say, 20 November 2026 is tested against donations made from 21 November 2025 to 20 November 2026 inclusive.
- Because the window moves, a company that has headroom today may lose it as earlier donations remain inside the window; headroom must be re-tested at each donation, not fixed annually.

**4.3 The ceiling is a single aggregate across all recipients.** "Other relevant donations" is defined by reference to donations "made by that company" (and group companies), not donations to the same recipient. *Ibid.*, s. 378(2). Accordingly the £5,000 is **not** £5,000 per party, **not** £5,000 per independent election candidate, and **not** £5,000 per accounting period. Donations to a party, to another political organisation and to an independent election candidate all count against the same £5,000.

**4.4 Group aggregation.** For a company that is **not** a subsidiary, the pot includes donations by that company and by any of its subsidiaries. For a company that **is** a subsidiary, the pot includes donations by that company, by any holding company of that company, and by any other subsidiary of any such holding company. *Ibid.*, s. 378(2)(a)–(b). The practical effect is that group companies share one £5,000 allowance in respect of a donation by a member of the group; a subsidiary cannot claim a fresh £5,000 independent of its holding company's donations.

**4.5 Knock-on for members' resolutions.** A donation exempt under section 378 is disregarded in determining what donations are authorised by a resolution passed for Part 14 purposes. *Ibid.*, s. 378(3). An exempt donation therefore neither consumes nor enlarges the authority conferred by a members' resolution.

**4.6 "Donation" is a defined term.** Section 378(2) defines "donation" for its own purposes as a donation to a political party or other political organisation or to an independent election candidate. The substantive meaning of "political donation" is supplied by cross-reference to the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 (2000 c. 41), ss. 50–53, which the Act applies with adaptation both to political parties/organisations and to independent election candidates; s. 53 of that Act governs the valuation of a donation. *Companies Act 2006*, Part 14, text as at 6 April 2026, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/part/14/2026-04-06 (definition provisions as reproduced there). **Caveat:** the retrieved extract does not display the section numbers of those definition provisions; they are conventionally cited as ss. 364–365 and should be pinned before the draft is finalised (§6.2 below). I have not read PPERA 2000 directly in preparing this note.

---

## 5. Corrections to the working assumptions

These are recorded expressly because the file's working assumptions were wrong and, if carried into advice, would produce an incorrect answer:

| Working assumption | Position on the text |
|---|---|
| "Measuring period is the company's accounting period" | **Wrong.** The period is the 12 months ending with the date the donation is made (s. 378(1)(b)). Nothing in s. 378 refers to accounting periods. |
| "Section 378 sits in Part 11, Chapter VI" | **Wrong.** Part 11 of the Act concerns derivative claims and proceedings by members. Section 378 sits in **Part 14** (Control of political donations and expenditure), in the group of sections headed "Exemptions" (ss. 376–378). |
| "Per candidate or per party" | **Neither.** A single aggregate £5,000 applies across all recipients (s. 378(1)–(2)). |
| "Figure may be index-linked" | **No indexation appears on the face of s. 378.** The £5,000 is a fixed statutory figure in the text as at 20 November 2026. Any uprating would require amendment, and none is disclosed (§3.2). |

---

## 6. Where the authority is thin, and what must be verified before reliance

**6.1 No judicial or official commentary located.** No case law construing section 378, and no explanatory notes for the section ("This section has no associated Explanatory Notes"), were located in the material retrieved. The analysis above is therefore textual only. *Companies Act 2006*, s. 378, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2014-06-13.

**6.2 Definition section numbers to be pinned.** The "political donation" definitions reproduced on the Part 14 page do not carry their section numbers in the retrieved extract; they should be confirmed as ss. 364–365 before citation in any filed document. *Companies Act 2006*, Part 14, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/part/14/2026-04-06.

**6.3 Northern Ireland and Scotland.** The section is marked "U.K." and so extends to all three jurisdictions, but the meaning of "political donation" is imported from PPERA 2000, whose application to Northern Ireland parties has a distinct statutory history. Do not assume the PPERA-based definition operates identically for a Northern Ireland-registered recipient without checking the PPERA 2000 text and its Northern Ireland provisions. Scottish recipients raise no separate devolution issue on the face of section 378, but the reserved/devolved boundary for party regulation should be confirmed if the donation is to a Scottish party.

**6.4 Unregistered companies.** Sections 362–379 are applied with modifications to unregistered companies by the Unregistered Companies Regulations 2009 (S.I. 2009/2436), regs. 3–5, Sch. 1 para. 9 (with transitional provisions and savings in regs. 7 and 9, Sch. 2). *Companies Act 2006*, s. 378, modification note C3, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2015-05-26/data.xht?view=snippet. If the company is unregistered, re-read the section as modified.

**6.5 Commencement.** Section 378 was wholly in force at 1 October 2008 (in force for certain purposes 1 October 2007 in England and Wales and 1 November 2007 in Northern Ireland), by S.I. 2007/2194, arts. 2(2), 3(1), 5(1)(i). *Ibid.*, commencement note I1.

**6.6 Separate PPERA reporting obligations not addressed.** Section 378 is an exemption from the *companies* authorisation requirement only. It does not displace any registration or reporting obligation owed to the Electoral Commission under PPERA 2000. Those thresholds are outside the scope of this note and are not stated here; they must be checked separately against PPERA 2000 and, for Northern Ireland, its separate provisions.

**6.7 Related Part 14 figures not stated.** Sections 366–367 (donations and expenditure requiring authorisation) and the resolution provisions of Part 14 use their own figures and their own periods. Nothing in this note should be read as stating those figures; only section 378 has been verified here.

---

## 7. Practical checklist for the company secretary

1. Identify the exact **date** the proposed donation will be made — that date fixes the 12-month look-back window.
2. Add up **all** donations (as defined) made by the company **and**, if it is a subsidiary, by its holding company and any other subsidiaries of that holding company, during the 12 months ending on that date.
3. Add the proposed donation. If the total is **£5,000 or less**, no Part 14 authorisation is needed. If it exceeds £5,000, authorisation is needed **for the excess only**.
4. Do not reset the calculation at the accounting reference date; re-run it at each donation.
5. Treat the £5,000 as one pot across all recipients — do not apply a separate £5,000 to each party or candidate.
6. Record exempt donations separately, because under s. 378(3) they are disregarded when determining what a members' resolution has authorised.
7. Check separately whether the donation triggers PPERA 2000 reporting to the Electoral Commission (§6.6).

---

## 8. Sources cited in full

1. **Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), section 378** — "Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month period U.K." Point-in-time view as at 13 June 2014. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2014-06-13 (accessed 23 November 2026).
2. **Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), Part 14** — "Control of political donations and expenditure", point-in-time view as at 6 April 2026 (reproducing s. 378 and the "political donation" definitions cross-referring to PPERA 2000 ss. 50–53). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/part/14/2026-04-06.
3. **Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), section 378** — snippet data view (commencement note I1; modification note C3). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2015-05-26/data.xht?view=snippet.
4. **Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), section 378** — point-in-time view as at 1 April 2025. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/cy/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2025-04-01.
5. **Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 (2000 c. 41), sections 50–53** — cross-referenced by Companies Act 2006, Part 14, for the meaning and valuation of a political donation (cited as cross-referenced; not read directly for this note).
6. **Companies Act 2006 (Commencement No. 3, Consequential Amendments, Transitional Provisions and Savings) Order 2007, S.I. 2007/2194**, arts. 2(2), 3(1), 5(1)(i) (commencement of s. 378).
7. **The Unregistered Companies Regulations 2009, S.I. 2009/2436**, regs. 3–5, Sch. 1 para. 9 (application of ss. 362–379 with modifications), with transitional provisions and savings in regs. 7, 9, Sch. 2.

---

DRAFT RESEARCH NOTE — FOR REVIEW BY A QUALIFIED ATTORNEY. THIS IS NOT LEGAL ADVICE.

Re: Minimum paid-up fraction on allotment of shares by a public company — section 586, Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46)
Jurisdiction: United Kingdom (England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland). The provision is marked with extent “U.K.”
Version relied on: Companies Act 2006, s. 586 as carried on legislation.gov.uk in the “latest available (revised)” version, stated to be up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 21 November 2026 — i.e. the version current on, and covering, the requested date of 20 November 2026. Fetched 23 November 2026.

1. QUESTION
What minimum paid-up fraction does s. 586 of the Companies Act 2006 require before a public company allots shares, on the text stated to be up to date through 20 November 2026?

2. SHORT ANSWER
One quarter — 25% — of the nominal value of each share allotted, and, cumulatively, the whole (100%) of any premium on that share. Companies Act 2006, s. 586(1). The section imposes no absolute monetary floor; the requirement is purely proportional to nominal value and premium. The requirement does not apply to shares allotted in pursuance of an employees' share scheme (s. 586(2)).

3. THE PROVISION IN FULL (as verified)
“586 Public companies: shares must be at least one-quarter paid up
U.K.
(1) A public company must not allot a share except as paid up at least as to one-quarter of its nominal value and the whole of any premium on it.
(2) This does not apply to shares allotted in pursuance of an employees' share scheme.
(3) If a company allots a share in contravention of this section—
(a) the share is to be treated as if one-quarter of its nominal value, together with the whole of any premium on it, had been received, and
(b) the allottee is liable to pay the company the minimum amount which should have been received in respect of the share under subsection (1) (less the value of any consideration actually applied in payment up, to any extent, of the share and any premium on it), with interest at the appropriate rate.
(4) Subsection (3) does not apply to the allotment of bonus shares, unless the allottee knew or ought to have known the shares were allotted in contravention of this section.”

4. ANALYSIS
4.1 Two cumulative limbs. Subsection (1) contains two distinct tests that must both be met on each share: (i) paid up as to at least one quarter of nominal value; and (ii) the whole of any premium paid up. They are joined by “and”, not “or”. A share that is 100% paid up as to nominal value but nil paid as to premium is non-compliant; a share that is fully paid as to premium but only 20% paid as to nominal value is non-compliant.
4.2 Measurement base. The fraction is measured against nominal value, not against issue price, market value or the amount of consideration agreed. Premium is measured against the premium actually agreed on that share. The words “of its nominal value” attach to the share, not to the class or to the company's aggregate capital.
4.3 Per share, at allotment. The prohibition is on allotting “a share except as paid up at least as to…”. The test is applied share by share and must be satisfied at the moment of allotment. A public company therefore cannot allot a share on the basis that the balance will be called later; if the s. 586 amount is not paid up at allotment, the allotment contravenes the section (with the consequences in 4.5 below). If a subscription is to be funded in tranches, the s. 586 amount must still be in place at allotment, or a different structure (e.g. a smaller nominal value, or a later allotment) should be used.
4.4 Employees' share scheme carve-out. Subsection (2) disapplies the whole of subsection (1) for shares allotted in pursuance of an employees' share scheme, so such shares may lawfully be allotted nil-paid or partly paid. The term “employees' share scheme” is a defined term in the Act (see the pointer at s. 1166 in section 9 below, not verified in this pass); the carve-out is not available merely because the allottee is an employee, and the scheme should be identified and documented in the board papers.
4.5 Effect of contravention. Section 586 creates no criminal offence of its own; its consequences are civil and are set out in subsections (3) and (4). On a contravening allotment: (a) the share is treated as if one quarter of nominal value plus the whole of the premium had been received — so the allotment is not void, and the capital and premium accounts are treated as credited accordingly; and (b) the allottee is personally liable to the company for the minimum amount that should have been received under subsection (1), less the value of any consideration actually applied in payment up, with interest at “the appropriate rate” (a defined term — see the s. 1173 pointer in section 9 below, not verified in this pass).
4.6 Bonus shares. Subsection (4) disapplies only subsection (3) — the consequence — for bonus shares, and only unless the allottee knew or ought to have known of the contravention. It does not disapply subsection (1). In practice bonus shares are capitalised fully paid out of reserves so the point rarely bites, but the drafting should not be read as a general exemption for bonus issues.
4.7 What the section does not require. It does not require full payment; it does not require payment of the balance within any period; and it does not set a monetary minimum (unlike, e.g., the separate “authorised minimum” share capital requirement for public companies, which is a registration/re-registration concept and not the s. 586 allotment rule — flagged but not verified in this pass, see section 9).

5. WORKED CALCULATIONS
Example A — 1,000 ordinary shares of £1.00 nominal, allotted at £2.50 (premium £1.50 per share).
  Nominal total £1,000; 25% = £250.
  Premium total £1,500; 100% = £1,500.
  Minimum paid up at allotment = £250 + £1,500 = £1,750.
  Cross-checks: £250 / £1,000 = 25% of nominal; £1,500 / £1,500 = 100% of premium; £1,750 / £2,500 issue price = 70%.
Example B — 10,000 shares of £0.10 nominal, allotted at par. Nominal £1,000; minimum = £250; no premium.
Example C — 1,000 £1.00 shares allotted at £2.50 with only £1,000 subscribed and applied. Nominal is fully paid but the premium is unpaid, so the allotment contravenes s. 586. Under s. 586(3)(a) the share is treated as if £1,750 had been received; under s. 586(3)(b) the allottee is liable for £1,750 − £1,000 = £750, plus interest at the appropriate rate. (This is my reading of the subsection on its face; no judicial construction of s. 586(3) has been located in this pass.)

6. VERSION CONTROL — CURRENCY OF THE TEXT (ask 2)
No page retrieved bears the literal phrase “up to date through 20 November 2026”. The pages retrieved state the following currency, and in every case subsections (1)–(4) are word-for-word identical:
  (a) Latest available (revised), https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/586 — “up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 21 November 2026”. This is a superset of 20 November 2026 and is the version relied on. Page digest recorded by the harness: 8436a63e2667 (truncated).
  (b) Point in time 06/04/2025, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/586/2025-04-06?view=extent&timeline=false — “on or before 23 November 2026”. Digest ba3e1054dc66.
  (c) Point in time 26/06/2017, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/586/2017-06-26 — “on or before 22 November 2026”. Digest dceb81463bca.
  (d) Point in time 01/10/2009 (Welsh/bilingual page), https://www.legislation.gov.uk/cy/ukpga/2006/46/section/586/2009-10-01 — “on or before 22 November 2026”. Digest fa98d09f0e8c.
  (e) Point in time 26/05/2008, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/586/2008-05-26 — “not valid for this point in time”, i.e. the section was not in force on that date. Digest 8f66cff11ff2.
  (f) Commercial reproduction (LexisNexis), https://www.lexisnexis.co.uk/legal/legislation/uk-parliament-acts/companies-act-2006-c46/part-17/section-586 — paywalled; the visible heading and subsection (1) match (a)–(e). Digest 6d9c836fd17e.
Conclusion on currency: the section is shown as valid from 1 October 2009, the only alternative version listed is the 01/10/2009 amendment, and no version anywhere in the timeline alters the one-quarter figure. The answer is therefore invariant across every candidate text bearing the requested currency date.

7. WHERE THE AUTHORITY IS THIN OR INCONSISTENT
7.1 The literal currency date does not appear on any page. The nearest statement is 21 November 2026 on the latest revised view. I have treated that as satisfying the instruction because it covers 20 November 2026 and because the wording is unchanged since 2009; the reviewer should note that the requester must confirm which source is said to bear the 20 November 2026 stamp.
7.2 Source metadata conflict. The 01/10/2009 page is labelled “no longer has effect” and states “No subsequent versions of this provision exist”, while the same site displays 2017, 2025 and latest versions. This is an editorial artefact of the point-in-time/Welsh view and does not affect the wording, but it should not be relied on as evidence that the section was repealed.
7.3 Outstanding unapplied change. The latest page lists, under “Changes and effects yet to be applied to Section 586”: “Sch. 11A para. 17E-17G substituted for Sch. 11A para. 17A-17D by 2026 c. 23 Sch. 36 para. 35”. This is a pending substitution of cross-referenced paragraphs in Schedule 11A; it does not touch the text of s. 586(1)–(4) and does not change the one-quarter figure.
7.4 Modification annotation. The section carries: “C2 Ss. 584-587 applied (12.5.2011) by The Companies Act 2006 (Consequential Amendments and Transitional Provisions) Order 2011 (S.I. 2011/1265), art. 5(1), Sch. 1 para. 9”. This is a “modification etc. (not altering text)” annotation applying ss. 584–587 to other bodies. If the allottee is not an ordinary UK public company (for example a body to which that Order applies), the reviewer should check the scope of that application before relying on this note.
7.5 Correction slip. The site lists “Correction Slip - 15/10/2010” against the Act. The text as displayed already reflects the revised version; no correction slip affects s. 586.
7.6 Absence of case law. No judicial decision construing s. 586 was located in this pass. The analysis in 4.5 and Example C is a reading of the statutory language, not an authoritative construction.
7.7 Thinness on definitions. The definitions of “employees' share scheme”, “the appropriate rate” and “public company” are assumed from the Act but were not re-verified in this pass (see section 9).

8. PRE-ALLOTMENT CHECKLIST (practical application)
Before the board allots:
  (1) Confirm the company is a public company within the Act (certificate of incorporation and s. 4 — flagged, verify).
  (2) Confirm whether any shares are to be allotted under an employees' share scheme; if yes, identify the scheme, record the s. 586(2) basis in the board minutes, and confirm no stricter rule applies in the articles.
  (3) For every other share, compute 25% of nominal value and add 100% of the agreed premium; record the per-share and per-class figures in the board minute.
  (4) Confirm that consideration equal to or exceeding that figure is actually applied in payment up at the moment of allotment (cleared funds for cash subscriptions; for non-cash consideration, confirm the amount credited as paid up, and check separately the public-company rules on non-cash consideration and valuation — flagged, verify).
  (5) Do not allot on the basis of uncalled or instalment funding; restructure instead.
  (6) Check the articles for any stricter paid-up requirement.
  (7) After allotment, make the return of allotments and update the register of members and confirmation statement (flagged, verify).

9. POINTERS FLAGGED BUT NOT VERIFIED IN THIS PASS
Companies Act 2006, s. 4 (meaning of “public company”); s. 91 (re-registration as a public company, which may impose a parallel paid-up test); s. 551 (authority to allot); s. 555 (return of allotment); s. 582 (payment up in money or money's worth); s. 593 (public company: valuation of non-cash consideration); s. 763 (the “authorised minimum” share capital, £50,000 — a separate registration requirement, not the s. 586 rule); s. 1166 (definition of “employees' share scheme”); s. 1173 (definition of “the appropriate rate”); s. 853A (confirmation statement). None of these is relied on to qualify the answer in section 2; they are listed so the reviewer can close them out.

10. CITATIONS IN FULL

answer:
# MEMORANDUM — WORD LIMITS FOR MOTION MEMORANDA UNDER 16 C.F.R. PART 3

**To:** Supervising Attorney (for review)
**Re:** Word limits applicable to memoranda supporting or opposing (a) a dispositive motion and (b) any other motion, in an FTC adjudicative proceeding under 16 C.F.R. Part 3 as in force on **November 21, 2026**
**Jurisdiction:** United States — federal administrative adjudication before the Federal Trade Commission (and its Administrative Law Judges) under the Commission's Rules of Practice, 16 C.F.R. pt. 3
**Status:** DRAFT for attorney review. Not legal advice.

---

## I. QUESTION PRESENTED

In an FTC adjudicative proceeding governed by 16 C.F.R. Part 3 as in force on 2026-11-21, what are the word limits for (1) memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, a dispositive motion, and (2) memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any other motion?

## II. SHORT ANSWER

| Paper | Word limit | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Memorandum **in support of, or in opposition to, a dispositive motion** | **10,000 words** | 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) (2026) |
| Memorandum **in support of, or in opposition to, any other motion** | **2,500 words** | 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) (2026) |
| *Reply* in support of a dispositive motion (separate limit — do not conflate) | 5,000 words | 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) (2026) |
| *Reply* in support of any other motion, where authorized by the ALJ or the Commission | 1,250 words | 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) (2026) |

The limits are stated in **words**, not pages. The rule expressly counts **headings, footnotes, and quotations** toward the limit, and expressly excludes the cover, tables of contents and of authorities, glossaries, statements regarding oral argument, addenda of statutes/rules/regulations, certificates of counsel, the proposed form of order, and any attachment required by § 3.45(e). 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) (2026).

The FTC's own contemporaneous statement equates these figures to roughly **40 double-spaced pages** (dispositive) and **10 double-spaced pages** (non-dispositive). 74 Fed. Reg. 1821 (Jan. 13, 2009).

## III. GOVERNING AUTHORITY (FULL CITATIONS)

1. **16 C.F.R. § 3.22, "Motions"** — 16 C.F.R. pt. 3, subpt. C (Adjudicative Proceedings), as set out in the Code of Federal Regulations, title 16, volume 1 (rev. Jan. 1, 2026), and as published in the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-3/subpart-C/section-3.22 (retrieved Nov. 23, 2026). Source note to the section: **74 Fed. Reg. 1821 (Jan. 13, 2009), as amended at 80 Fed. Reg. 15160 (Mar. 23, 2015)**.
2. **74 Fed. Reg. 1821 (Jan. 13, 2009)** — FTC final rule amending 16 C.F.R. Parts 3 and 4 (the rulemaking that adopted the word limits), FTC posted document "090113rulesofpractice.pdf," https://www.ftc.gov/sites/default/files/documents/federal_register_notices/rules-practice-16-cfr-parts-3-and-4/090113rulesofpractice.pdf.
3. **16 C.F.R. § 3.26** (summary decision) — cross-references § 3.22(c) for memoranda filed with a summary-decision motion.
4. **16 C.F.R. § 3.31(e)** (motions to dismiss after denial of preliminary injunctive relief) — independent 10,000-word limit.
5. **16 C.F.R. § 3.52** (appeal from initial decision) — 14,000-word principal/answering brief; 7,000-word reply; 16,500-word cross-appeal brief. *Different procedural stage; not a motion limit.*
6. **FTC Press Release, "FTC Issues Interim Final Rules Amending Parts 3 and 4 of its Rules of Practice…" (Dec. 23, 2008)**, https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2008/12/ftc-issues-interim-final-rules-amending-parts-3-4-its-rules-practice-rules-are-designed-expedite (secondary/agency description; used only for context, not as the source of the numbers).

## IV. ANALYSIS

### A. The operative text

Section 3.22(c), captioned "Content," provides in relevant part:

> "All written motions shall state the particular order, ruling, or action desired and the grounds therefor. **Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any dispositive motion shall not exceed 10,000 words. Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any other motion shall not exceed 2,500 words.** Any reply in support of a dispositive motion shall not exceed 5,000 words and any reply in support of any other motion authorized by the Administrative Law Judge or the Commission shall not exceed 1,250 words. These word count limitations include headings, footnotes, and quotations, but do not include the cover, table of contents, table of citations or authorities, glossaries, statements with respect to oral argument, any addendums containing statutes, rules or regulations, any certificates of counsel, proposed form of order, and any attachment required by § 3.45(e). Documents that fail to comply with these provisions shall not be filed with the Secretary."

— 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) (2026). The same sentence pair appears verbatim in the 2023 codification (16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) (2023)) and in the Federal Register document that adopted it (74 Fed. Reg. 1821), where the Commission recorded that it "received no comments on these word count limitations and they have been adopted as proposed."

### B. Dispositive motions — 10,000 words

The 10,000-word ceiling attaches to the *memorandum*, i.e., the brief filed with the motion or the opposition, not to the motion paper itself. Section 3.22(c) does not impose a word cap on the motion document (it imposes content requirements: the relief sought, the grounds, a draft order, and counsel's contact information). The clearest Part 3 exemplars of a "dispositive motion" are:

- **Motions for summary decision** under 16 C.F.R. § 3.26, which expressly direct that "[t]he parties may file memoranda of law in support of, or in opposition to, the motion consistent with § 3.22(c)"; and
- **Motions to dismiss** the administrative complaint, including the post-preliminary-injunction motion under 16 C.F.R. § 3.31, which carries its **own, parallel** 10,000-word limit in § 3.31(e) ("Memoranda in support of or in opposition to motions authorized by this section shall not exceed 10,000 words").

Because § 3.31(e) supplies the limit for § 3.31 motions directly, cite **§ 3.31(e)** for that motion and **§ 3.22(c)** for summary-decision and other dispositive motion memoranda. The numbers are the same (10,000), so the citation choice does not change the page budget.

### C. Any other motion — 2,500 words

All non-dispositive motion memoranda — motions to compel or determine sufficiency (§ 3.38(a)), motions for sanctions (§ 3.38(b)), motions for enforcement (§ 3.38(c)), motions to quash (§ 3.34(c)), motions in limine, motions for extension, and similar — are capped at **2,500 words**. Note the additional, independent obligations that attach to several of these: a meet-and-confer statement is required for motions to quash, to compel/determine sufficiency, for sanctions, and for enforcement, 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(g) ("shall recite the date, time, and place of each such conference between counsel, and the names of all parties participating in each such conference"), and that statement counts toward the word budget unless it is filed as a separate certificate.

### D. Replies — separate figures

- Reply in support of a **dispositive** motion: **5,000 words**.
- Reply in support of **any other** motion: **1,250 words**, and only where "authorized by the Administrative Law Judge or the Commission" — i.e., there is no automatic reply right on a non-dispositive motion.

16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c). The 2009 rulemaking describes the design: an automatic right of reply for dispositive motions, with replies and surreplies on non-dispositive motions "permitted only in circumstances where the parties wish to draw the ALJ's or the Commission's attention to recent important developments or controlling authority that could not have been raised earlier in the party's principal brief," plus a five-day filing deadline for any authorized reply. 74 Fed. Reg. 1821.

### E. What counts toward the limit

**Counted:** headings, footnotes, quotations. § 3.22(c).
**Not counted:** cover; table of contents; table of citations/authorities; glossaries; statements with respect to oral argument; addenda containing statutes, rules, or regulations; certificates of counsel; proposed form of order; any attachment required by § 3.45(e). § 3.22(c).

Practical consequence: the two most common ways to blow the budget are (i) extensive string citations inside footnotes and (ii) block quotations from the administrative complaint or prior orders — both count.

### F. Consequence of non-compliance

The rule is self-executing at the filing window: "Documents that fail to comply with these provisions **shall not be filed with the Secretary**." 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c). This is a filing bar, not a discretionary sanction; a compliant re-filing after the deadline would require relief from the ALJ or the Commission.

### G. Related limits that must not be confused with § 3.22(c)

| Provision | Paper | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| § 3.22(c) | Motion memoranda (dispositive / other) | 10,000 / 2,500 words |
| § 3.22(c) | Replies (dispositive / other) | 5,000 / 1,250 words |
| § 3.31(e) | Memoranda on motions to dismiss after denial of a preliminary injunction | 10,000 words |
| § 3.52 | Appeal briefs (principal/answering; reply; cross-appeal) | 14,000; 7,000; 16,500 words |

Section 3.52 limits govern **appeals from the initial decision**, a different stage of the proceeding, and are cited here only to prevent a mis-citation.

## V. VERSION VERIFICATION AND RESIDUAL RISK

1. **Three-way textual concordance.** The 10,000/2,500 figures are identical in (a) the eCFR "current" text retrieved 2026-11-23, (b) the GovInfo CFR 2026 title 16 volume (verdate Aug. 25, 2026), and (c) the GovInfo CFR 2023 XML — and match the 2009 adopting rule. The word-limit sentences have therefore been stable across the entire 2009–2026 span for which text was retrieved.
2. **Two-day currency gap.** The eCFR capture is dated 2026-11-23, two days *after* the target date of 2026-11-21. If an amendment to § 3.22 took effect on 2026-11-22, the retrieved "current" text would not reflect the 2026-11-21 state. **Recommended closing step:** run a point-in-time eCFR query ("Date: 2026-11-21") on § 3.22 and confirm the section's source note still reads "74 FR 1821, Jan. 13, 2009, as amended at 80 FR 15160, Mar. 23, 2015," with no later amendment. The section's own source note, as retrieved, lists **no amendment after March 23, 2015**, which is strong but not conclusive evidence for the target date.
3. **No express waiver mechanism in the retrieved text.** Section 3.22(c) says the memoranda "shall not exceed" the stated counts and contains no "unless otherwise ordered" clause for those counts (contrast the reply provision, which conditions non-dispositive replies on ALJ/Commission authorization). I have **not** retrieved § 3.1 (definitions) or § 3.21 (scheduling order), so I do not assert whether a general modification power exists. Treat the limits as **firm** and seek relief prospectively if a longer brief is genuinely required.
4. **"Dispositive motion" is not defined in the retrieved text.** Part 3 uses the term without a definition in § 3.22. The safe reading covers motions that can end the proceeding or a claim in it (summary decision under § 3.26; dismissal under § 3.22(a) and § 3.31). For a motion of doubtful character (e.g., a motion to strike an affirmative defense, a motion for judgment on the pleadings), brief to the **2,500-word** limit and seek leave to exceed, rather than risk the filing bar under § 3.22(c).
5. **Standing orders / ALJ orders.** Individual ALJs may issue scheduling or standing orders in a particular matter. Section 3.22(c) does not itself authorize a departure, but a scheduling order may set a *shorter* deadline, and any party should confirm the docketed scheduling order before finalizing length.

## VI. COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST FOR THE FILING

- [ ] Word count of the memorandum, **including headings, footnotes, and quotations**, is ≤ 10,000 (dispositive) or ≤ 2,500 (other).
- [ ] Count taken from the word processor's count on the body-plus-footnotes, after removing the excluded front/back matter.
- [ ] Excluded matter actually excluded: cover, TOC, table of authorities, glossary, oral-argument statement, statutory/regulatory addenda, certificate of counsel, proposed form of order, § 3.45(e) attachment.
- [ ] Motion itself states the particular order, ruling, or action desired and the grounds; attaches a draft order containing the proposed relief; includes counsel's name, address, telephone, fax, and email. § 3.22(c).
- [ ] Meet-and-confer statement attached, if the motion is one of those listed in § 3.22(g).
- [ ] If a reply: ≤ 5,000 (dispositive) or ≤ 1,250 and authorized (other).
- [ ] If the motion is a § 3.31 motion: cite § 3.31(e) and confirm 10,000 words.
- [ ] Docketed scheduling order checked for any case-specific modification of deadlines or length.

## VII. CAVEATS

This memorandum is a draft prepared for review by a qualified attorney. It is not legal advice. It states the law of the United States federal administrative system only, and only for adjudicative proceedings under 16 C.F.R. Part 3; it does not address consent-order practice, Part 2 proceedings, or any state or foreign regime, where different limits may apply. The figures should be re-verified against the point-in-time eCFR text for 2026-11-21 before any brief is finalized.

The first reads: "Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any dispositive motion shall not exceed 10,000 words."

DRAFT FOR REVIEW BY A QUALIFIED ATTORNEY — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

MATTER: Withdrawal instructions for an online retailer. Question: when does the withdrawal period expire (1) for a service contract and (2) for a sales contract?

JURISDICTION: European Union. The governing instrument is a Directive, not a Regulation: the rules that bind a given consumer are those of the Member State whose law implements it. The answers below state the Directive's baseline. The national implementing measure of the Member State(s) into which the retailer sells must be checked before publication; the Directive is a minimum-harmonisation instrument in several respects and expressly leaves certain points (day-counting, non-working days) to national law.

PRIMARY SOURCES
[PS1] Directive 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 October 2011 on consumer rights, amending Council Directive 93/13/EEC and Directive 1999/44/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Council Directive 85/577/EEC and Directive 97/7/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council, OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64–88; CELEX 32011L0083.
[PS2] Directive (EU) 2019/2161 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2019 amending Council Directive 93/13/EEC and Directives 98/6/EC, 2005/29/EC and 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards the better enforcement and modernisation of Union consumer protection rules, OJ L 328, 18.12.2019, p. 7–28; CELEX 32019L2161.
[PS3] Directive (EU) 2019/771 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2019 on certain aspects concerning contracts for the sale of goods, amending Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 and Directive 2009/22/EC, and repealing Directive 1999/44/EC, OJ L 136, 22.5.2019, p. 28–50; CELEX 32019L0771.
[PS4] Regulation (EEC, Euratom) No 1182/71 of the Council of 3 June 1971 determining the rules applicable to periods, dates and time limits, OJ L 124, 8.6.1971, p. 1–2; CELEX 31971R1182.

Version note: the operative text is [PS1] as amended by [PS2]. In the consolidated CELEX text, the provisions inserted or replaced by [PS2] carry the consolidation marker "▼M2". Citations below are to the consolidated text.

=====================================================================
SECTION 1 — THE ANSWERS
=====================================================================

1.1 SERVICE CONTRACT — the withdrawal period expires at the end of 14 days from the day of the conclusion of the contract. Source: Article 9(2)(a) of [PS1] ("in the case of service contracts, the day of the conclusion of the contract"), read with Article 9(1) of [PS1].

1.2 SALES CONTRACT — the withdrawal period expires at the end of 14 days from the day on which the consumer, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer, acquires physical possession of the goods. Source: Article 9(2)(b) of [PS1], read with Article 9(1) of [PS1].

1.3 Both answers are subject to Article 10 of [PS1] (omission of the information on the right of withdrawal), which extends the period to 12 months and can restart it for a further 14 days — Section 5 below. Both are also subject to the 30-day option in Article 9(1a) of [PS1], inserted by [PS2], where the applicable national law has taken that option up — paragraph 3.2 below.

=====================================================================
SECTION 2 — THE GOVERNING TEXT
=====================================================================

2.1 Article 9(1) of [PS1]: "The consumer shall have a period of 14 days to withdraw from a distance or off-premises contract, without giving any reason, and without incurring any costs other than those provided for in Article 13(2) and Article 14."

2.2 Article 9(2) of [PS1] (as consolidated): "Without prejudice to Article 10, the withdrawal period referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article shall expire after 14 days or, in cases where Member States have adopted rules in accordance with paragraph 1a of this Article, 30 days from:
(a) in the case of service contracts, the day of the conclusion of the contract;
(b) in the case of sales contracts, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the goods or:
(i) in the case of multiple goods ordered by the consumer in one order and delivered separately, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the last good;
(ii) in the case of delivery of a good consisting of multiple lots or pieces, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the last lot or piece;
(iii) in the case of contracts for regular delivery of goods during defined period of time, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the first good;
(c) in the case of contracts for the supply of water, gas or electricity, where they are not put up for sale in a limited volume or set quantity, of district heating or of digital content which is not supplied on a tangible medium, the day of the conclusion of the contract."

2.3 Article 10 of [PS1] (as consolidated): "Omission of information on the right of withdrawal
1. If the trader has not provided the consumer with the information on the right of withdrawal as required by point (h) of Article 6(1), the withdrawal period shall expire 12 months from the end of the initial withdrawal period, as determined in accordance with Article 9(2).
2. If the trader has provided the consumer with the information provided for in paragraph 1 of this Article within 12 months from the day referred to in Article 9(2), the withdrawal period shall expire 14 days or, in cases where Member States have adopted rules in accordance with Article 9(1a), 30 days after the day upon which the consumer receives that information."

2.4 Article 6(1) of [PS1], chapeau: the information listed in points (a) to (t) must be given "Before the consumer is bound by a distance or off-premises contract, or any corresponding offer ... in a clear and comprehensible manner". Point (h) is "where a right of withdrawal exists, the conditions, time limit and procedures for exercising that right in accordance with Article 9(1), as well as the model withdrawal form set out in Annex I(B)".

2.5 Article 6(4) of [PS1]: "The information referred to in points (h), (i) and (j) of paragraph 1 of this Article may be provided by means of the model instructions on withdrawal set out in Annex I(A). The trader shall have fulfilled the information requirements laid down in points (h), (i) and (j) of paragraph 1 of this Article if the trader has supplied these instructions to the consumer, correctly filled in. The references to the withdrawal period of 14 days in the model instructions on withdrawal set out in Annex I(A) shall be replaced by references to a withdrawal period of 30 days in cases where Member States have adopted rules in accordance with Article 9(1a)."

2.6 Article 6(6) of [PS1]: "If the trader has not complied with the information requirements on additional charges or other costs as referred to in point (e) of paragraph 1, or on the costs of returning the goods as referred to in point (i) of paragraph 1, the consumer shall not bear those charges or costs."

2.7 Article 6(9) of [PS1]: the burden of proof in respect of compliance with the information requirements laid down in Chapter III is on the trader.

2.8 Article 7(3) of [PS1]: "Where a consumer wants the performance of services, or the supply of water, gas or electricity, where they are not put up for sale in a limited volume or set quantity, or of district heating to begin during the withdrawal period provided for in Article 9(2), and the contract places the consumer under an obligation to pay, the trader shall require that the consumer make such an express request on a durable medium and request the consumer to acknowledge that, once the contract has been fully performed by the trader, the consumer will no longer have the right of withdrawal."

2.9 Article 16(a) of [PS1]: Member States shall not provide for the right of withdrawal set out in Articles 9 to 15 in respect of distance and off-premises contracts as regards "service contracts after the service has been fully performed if the performance has begun with the consumer's prior express consent, and with the acknowledgement that he will lose his right of withdrawal once the contract has been fully performed by the trader". The list in Article 16 is closed for distance and off-premises contracts.

2.10 Article 14(3) of [PS1]: where the consumer exercises the right of withdrawal after having made a request in accordance with Article 7(3) or Article 8(8), the consumer pays an amount proportionate to what has been provided until the consumer informed the trader of the withdrawal, in comparison with the full coverage of the contract.

2.11 Article 13(1) of [PS1]: the trader reimburses all payments received from the consumer, including, where applicable, the costs of delivery, without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days from the day on which the trader is informed of the consumer's decision to withdraw.

2.12 Article 2 of [PS1], definitions: "'sales contract' means any contract under which the trader transfers or undertakes to transfer the ownership of goods to the consumer and the consumer pays or undertakes to pay the price thereof, including any contract having as its object both goods and services"; "'service contract' means any contract other than a sales contract under which the trader supplies or undertakes to supply a service to the consumer and the consumer pays or undertakes to pay the price thereof".

=====================================================================
SECTION 3 — SERVICE CONTRACTS: RULE, FORMULA, EARLY EXTINCTION
=====================================================================

3.1 Trigger. The period runs from the day of the conclusion of the contract (Article 9(2)(a) of [PS1]). It does not run from the day performance begins, from the day the consumer pays, or from the day the consumer first uses the service. For an online retailer, the date of conclusion is determined by the applicable national law of contract formation (offer/acceptance, order confirmation), which is a national-law question outside the Directive and must be fixed in the retailer's terms so that the date is objectively ascertainable.

3.2 Length. 14 days (Article 9(1) and 9(2) of [PS1]). 30 days applies only if the Member State has adopted rules under Article 9(1a) of [PS1] (inserted by [PS2]); where it has, every reference to 14 days in Articles 9 and 10 and in Annex I(A) is replaced by 30 days (Article 6(4) third sentence and Article 10(2) of [PS1]). Do not use 30 days unless the applicable national law has taken up that option.

3.3 Formula. Expiry = C + N, where C = the date of conclusion of the contract and N = 14 days (30 days only under Article 9(1a)). The period expires at the end of the last day. Day-counting convention: Section 6.

3.4 The period can be cut short, and the right lost, before the 14 days run out. Under Article 16(a) of [PS1], the right of withdrawal does not exist for a service contract once the service has been fully performed, provided (i) performance began with the consumer's prior express consent and (ii) the consumer acknowledged that the right is lost on full performance. Article 7(3) of [PS1] prescribes how the trader must obtain those two elements for a distance contract: the consumer must make an express request on a durable medium to begin performance during the withdrawal period, and the trader must request the acknowledgement. Consequences for drafting:
  (a) A request for early performance, standing alone, does not extinguish the right. A request plus performance begun but not completed does not extinguish the right either: Article 16(a) requires full performance. The right survives until the service is fully performed or the 14 days expire, whichever is first.
  (b) If the trader has not obtained the express request on a durable medium and the acknowledgement, Article 16(a) does not apply, the right survives the full 14 days, and Article 14(3) does not apply either — so no proportionate payment is owed for the pre-withdrawal period.
  (c) For continuing services (e.g. a 12-month subscription), full performance is not reached during the withdrawal period, so the right is never extinguished early by Article 16(a); the consumer who withdraws after performance has begun owes the proportionate amount under Article 14(3), and the Annex I(A) sentence in paragraph 7.1(c) below must be included.
  (d) Illustration: contract concluded 1 March 2025; consumer expressly requests on a durable medium on 3 March that performance begin and acknowledges loss of the right; service fully performed on 10 March. The right of withdrawal is extinguished on 10 March 2025, five days before the 14-day period would otherwise have expired. If instead the service is only partly performed by 12 March and the consumer withdraws on 12 March, the right subsists and Article 14(3) applies.

3.5 Worked example (service contract concluded 1 March 2025, 14-day baseline):
  - Convention A (trigger day not counted): days 1–14 are 2 to 15 March 2025; the period expires at the end of 15 March 2025.
  - Convention B (trigger day counted): days 1–14 are 1 to 14 March 2025; the period expires at the end of 14 March 2025.
  (Conventions defined in Section 6.)

=====================================================================
SECTION 4 — SALES CONTRACTS: RULE, FORMULA, SUB-CASES, NON-DELIVERY
=====================================================================

4.1 Trigger. Physical possession. The period runs from the day on which the consumer, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer, acquires physical possession of the goods (Article 9(2)(b) of [PS1]). Two points follow from the words used:
  (a) Handing the goods to the carrier is not the trigger. Delivery to a locker, to a pick-up point, or to a neighbour counts only if the neighbour is a third party indicated by the consumer — the carrier and its agents are expressly excluded.
  (b) Where the consumer indicates a third party (e.g. a gift recipient), that third party's possession starts the period.

4.2 Sub-cases under Article 9(2)(b)(i)–(iii) of [PS1]:
  (i) multiple goods ordered in one order and delivered separately — the day the consumer acquires physical possession of the LAST good;
  (ii) a good consisting of multiple lots or pieces — the day the consumer acquires physical possession of the LAST lot or piece;
  (iii) contracts for regular delivery of goods during a defined period — the day the consumer acquires physical possession of the FIRST good.

4.3 Goods supplied as water, gas or electricity (not put up for sale in a limited volume or set quantity), district heating, or digital content not supplied on a tangible medium: the trigger is the day of the conclusion of the contract (Article 9(2)(c) of [PS1]). Where the retailer sells digital content not on a tangible medium, the trigger is therefore the conclusion date, not a download date, and Article 16(m) of [PS1] governs the separate question of when the right is lost for such content.

4.4 Mixed contracts. A contract with both goods and services as its object is a sales contract under the Article 2 definition in [PS1] ("including any contract having as its object both goods and services"). The delivery trigger in Article 9(2)(b) therefore applies to a bundle of, say, a device plus an installation or a subscription. Where the service element is to begin within the withdrawal period, Article 7(3) of [PS1] still applies to that element.

4.5 Non-delivery — correction of a premise in the instructions. There is no rule that a trader's failure to deliver within the withdrawal period extends the period to 12 months. Article 10 of [PS1] has only two paragraphs (the consolidated text moves directly from Article 10(2) to the heading of Article 11), and [PS2] amended Article 10(2) only. On the Directive's text, if physical possession is never acquired, the Article 9(2)(b) trigger never occurs and the 14-day withdrawal period never begins to run; the consumer's remedy for non-delivery lies in [PS3] and the applicable national law, not in an extension of the withdrawal period. A national implementing measure could in principle add a fallback trigger, which is a point to check — but it cannot be assumed.

4.6 Worked examples (14-day baseline):
  - Single good, possession acquired 1 March 2025: Convention A → expiry end of 15 March 2025; Convention B → expiry end of 14 March 2025.
  - Multiple goods in one order delivered separately, last good possessed 20 April 2025: Convention A → 21–30 April (10 days) + 1–4 May (4 days) = 14; expiry end of 4 May 2025. Convention B → 20–30 April (11 days) + 1–3 May (3 days) = 14; expiry end of 3 May 2025.
  - Regular delivery during a defined period, first good possessed 1 March 2025: expiry as for the single good above, regardless of how many later deliveries follow.

=====================================================================
SECTION 5 — THE ARTICLE 10 EXTENSION (BOTH CONTRACT TYPES)
=====================================================================

5.1 Initial period omitted information — Article 10(1) of [PS1]. If the trader has not provided the information required by Article 6(1)(h), the period expires 12 months from the END of the initial withdrawal period determined under Article 9(2). Note the anchor: it is the end of the initial period, not the trigger day.

5.2 Late provision within the window — Article 10(2) of [PS1]. If the trader provides that information within 12 months from the DAY referred to in Article 9(2) (i.e. from the trigger day), the period expires 14 days (30 days where Article 9(1a) has been adopted) after the day the consumer receives the information. Note the different anchor from Article 10(1).

5.3 Outer bound. The two paragraphs meet at the same instant: under Article 10(1) the period cannot run beyond trigger day + 14 days + 12 months; under Article 10(2) the latest possible restart is at trigger day + 12 months, giving expiry at trigger day + 12 months + 14 days. Information supplied after the 12-month window does not restart anything, because the period will already have expired under Article 10(1).

5.4 Worked example (service contract concluded 1 March 2025, no Article 6(1)(h) information supplied with the contract):
  - Convention A: initial period ends 15 March 2025; extended expiry end of 15 March 2026 (the outer bound).
  - Convention B: initial period ends 14 March 2025; extended expiry end of 14 March 2026.
  - If the information is received by the consumer on 10 June 2025 (within 12 months of 1 March 2025), the period expires 14 days after receipt: Convention A → 24 June 2025; Convention B → 23 June 2025.
  - If the information is received on 20 March 2026 (after the window), nothing restarts; the period expired on 15 March 2026 (Convention A).

5.5 Burden of proof. Under Article 6(9) of [PS1] the burden of proving that the Article 6(1)(h) information was supplied is on the trader. The retailer must therefore retain evidence of what was shown to the consumer, and when, at the pre-contractual stage.

5.6 Timing of the information. Article 6(1) of [PS1] requires the information to be given before the consumer is bound. Supplying the Annex I(A) instructions only in the post-contractual confirmation on a durable medium (Article 8(7) of [PS1]) is, on the conservative reading, not compliance with Article 6(1)(h), and would expose the retailer to the Article 10(1) extension. The instructions should be given before the order is placed and repeated in the confirmation.

5.7 Safe harbour. Under Article 6(4) of [PS1], supplying the Annex I(A) model instructions correctly filled in discharges the Article 6(1)(h), (i) and (j) duties. The wording in Section 7 is taken from Annex I(A) and should be used verbatim, with only the bracketed fields completed.

=====================================================================
SECTION 6 — COUNTING THE DAYS AND THE LAST DAY (FLAGGED, NOT RESOLVED)
=====================================================================

6.1 The Directive fixes the number of days and the trigger event. It does not lay down a method of counting: whether the trigger day itself counts, and how a last day falling on a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday is treated, are matters for the national law implementing [PS1]. [PS4] does not supply the answer, because it governs periods laid down in acts of the Union institutions, not periods fixed by a private contract under a directive.

6.2 Two conventions are in use, and the retailer's instructions must be consistent with whichever the governing national law adopts:
  - Convention A (trigger day not counted): day 1 is the day after the trigger; the period expires at the end of the 14th day after the trigger.
  - Convention B (trigger day counted): day 1 is the trigger day; the period expires at the end of the 14th day counting the trigger day.
  Every worked example in Sections 3, 4 and 5 is given under both conventions so that no figure in this draft depends on the point being resolved. The reviewing attorney should fix one convention per target market and strike the other.

6.3 The last day. Whether the period is extended where the last day is a non-working day, and whether public holidays in the consumer's Member State count, are national-law points. Flagged for confirmation.

6.4 Exercise before expiry. Article 11(1) of [PS1] requires the consumer to inform the trader of the decision to withdraw before the expiry of the period, using the Annex I(B) model form or any other unequivocal statement. The Annex I(A) instructions state that it is sufficient to send the communication before the period expires; that sentence must be retained verbatim.

=====================================================================
SECTION 7 — DRAFT WITHDRAWAL INSTRUCTIONS FOR INSERTION INTO THE RETAILER'S TERMS
=====================================================================

(Annex I(A) wording of [PS1], completed. Use the version that matches the contract; delete the alternatives. Where the applicable national law has adopted Article 9(1a) of [PS1], replace every "14 days" below with "30 days".)

7.1 SERVICE CONTRACT (and digital content not supplied on a tangible medium, and water/gas/electricity/district heating under Article 9(2)(c))

"Right of withdrawal
You have the right to withdraw from this contract within 14 days without giving any reason.
The withdrawal period will expire after 14 days from the day of the conclusion of the contract.
To exercise the right of withdrawal, you must inform us [trader's name, geographical address, telephone number and e-mail address] of your decision to withdraw from this contract by an unequivocal statement (e.g. a letter sent by post or e-mail). You may use the attached model withdrawal form, but it is not obligatory. You can also electronically fill in and submit the model withdrawal form or any other unequivocal statement on our website [internet address]. If you use this option, we will communicate to you an acknowledgement of receipt of such a withdrawal on a durable medium (e.g. by e-mail) without delay.
To meet the withdrawal deadline, it is sufficient for you to send your communication concerning your exercise of the right of withdrawal before the withdrawal period has expired.

Effects of withdrawal
If you withdraw from this contract, we shall reimburse to you all payments received from you, without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days from the day on which we are informed about your decision to withdraw from this contract. We will carry out such reimbursement using the same means of payment as you used for the initial transaction, unless you have expressly agreed otherwise; in any event, you will not incur any fees as a result of such reimbursement.
If you requested to begin the performance of services during the withdrawal period, you shall pay us an amount which is in proportion to what has been provided until you have communicated us your withdrawal from this contract, in comparison with the full coverage of the contract."

Drafting notes to 7.1:
  (a) The final sentence tracks Article 14(3) of [PS1] and must appear wherever the retailer accepts an Article 7(3) express request for early performance. If the retailer does not accept early performance, delete the sentence and do not solicit the request.
  (b) The paragraph on the Article 16(a) loss of the right does not belong in the Annex I(A) block; if early performance is offered, put the Article 7(3) request and acknowledgement in a separate, separately-ticked checkout step, on a durable medium, and confirm it to the consumer under Article 8(7) of [PS1].
  (c) The "14 days" in the reimbursement paragraph is the Article 13(1) period and is a different period from the withdrawal period; do not change one without the other.

7.2 SALES CONTRACT — single good

"Right of withdrawal
You have the right to withdraw from this contract within 14 days without giving any reason.
The withdrawal period will expire after 14 days from the day on which you acquire, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you acquires, physical possession of the goods.
To exercise the right of withdrawal, you must inform us [trader's name, geographical address, telephone number and e-mail address] of your decision to withdraw from this contract by an unequivocal statement (e.g. a letter sent by post or e-mail). You may use the attached model withdrawal form, but it is not obligatory. You can also electronically fill in and submit the model withdrawal form or any other unequivocal statement on our website [internet address]. If you use this option, we will communicate to you an acknowledgement of receipt of such a withdrawal on a durable medium (e.g. by e-mail) without delay.
To meet the withdrawal deadline, it is sufficient for you to send your communication concerning your exercise of the right of withdrawal before the withdrawal period has expired.

Effects of withdrawal
If you withdraw from this contract, we shall reimburse to you all payments received from you, including the costs of delivery (with the exception of the supplementary costs resulting from your choice of a type of delivery other than the least expensive type of standard delivery offered by us), without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days from the day on which we are informed about your decision to withdraw from this contract. We will carry out such reimbursement using the same means of payment as you used for the initial transaction, unless you have expressly agreed otherwise; in any event, you will not incur any fees as a result of such reimbursement.
We may withhold reimbursement until we have received the goods back or you have supplied evidence of having sent back the goods, whichever is the earliest.
You will have to bear the direct cost of returning the goods. [Alternative where the retailer bears them: We will bear the direct cost of returning the goods.]
You are only liable for any diminished value of the goods resulting from the handling other than what is necessary to establish the nature, characteristics and functioning of the goods."

7.3 SALES CONTRACT — the three sub-cases. Replace the second sentence of 7.2 with the following, as applicable:
  - multiple goods ordered in one order and delivered separately: "The withdrawal period will expire after 14 days from the day on which you acquire, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you acquires, physical possession of the last good."
  - a good consisting of multiple lots or pieces: "... physical possession of the last lot or piece."
  - regular delivery of goods during a defined period of time: "... physical possession of the first good."

7.4 MIXED GOODS-AND-SERVICES CONTRACT. Use 7.2 or 7.3 for the goods element (the contract is a sales contract under Article 2 of [PS1]) and add the Article 14(3) sentence from 7.1 only if early performance of the service element is offered and requested under Article 7(3).

7.5 MODEL WITHDRAWAL FORM (Annex I(B) of [PS1]) — to be attached to the instructions:

"Model withdrawal form
(complete and return this form only if you wish to withdraw from the contract)
— To [trader's name, geographical address and e-mail address]:
— I/We (*) hereby give notice that I/We (*) withdraw from my/our (*) contract of sale of the following goods (*)/for the provision of the following service (*),
— Ordered on (*)/received on (*),
— Name of consumer(s),
— Address of consumer(s),
— Signature of consumer(s) (only if this form is notified on paper),
— Date
(*) Delete as appropriate."

Note: Article 11(1) of [PS1] prohibits Member States from imposing formal requirements on the model form beyond those in Annex I(B). Do not add fields.

=====================================================================
SECTION 8 — CONFIRM BEFORE PUBLICATION (REVIEWING ATTORNEY)
=====================================================================

1. Identify the Member State(s) of the consumers targeted and obtain the implementing measure (for example, and to be verified rather than assumed: in Ireland, the European Union (Consumer Information, Cancellation and Other Rights) Regulations 2013; in Germany, §§ 312g, 355 and 356 BGB; in France, the Code de la consommation). Confirm the implementing text of Article 9(2), Article 10 and Annex I(A).
2. Confirm whether the Member State has adopted rules under Article 9(1a) of [PS1] (30-day period). If so, replace every "14 days" in Section 7 and every "N = 14" in Sections 3 to 5.
3. Fix the day-counting convention (Section 6.2) and the treatment of the last day falling on a non-working day or public holiday (Section 6.3) for each target market.
4. Confirm the contract-formation rule that fixes the "day of the conclusion of the contract" for the service contract, and make the checkout record the date unambiguously.
5. Confirm the delivery and possession evidence trail for the sales contract, including the identity of any third party indicated by the consumer and the treatment of split deliveries and partial shipments.
6. Confirm the Article 7(3) request-and-acknowledgement flow, its durable-medium record, and the Article 8(7) confirmation.
7. Confirm that the Annex I(A) and Annex I(B) text in Section 7 is verbatim against the consolidated text of [PS1] as amended by [PS2] at the date of publication.
8. Confirm that the pre-contractual information is delivered before the consumer is bound (Article 6(1) of [PS1]), not only in the post-contractual confirmation.
9. Confirm the record-keeping that discharges the Article 6(9) burden of proof.
10. Confirm whether any Member State has added a fallback trigger for goods never delivered (Section 4.5).

=====================================================================
SECTION 9 — CORRECTIONS TO THE INSTRUCTIONS GIVEN WITH THIS MATTER
=====================================================================

9.1 "Article 10(3) extends the period to 12 months where the trader fails to deliver within the withdrawal period" — there is no Article 10(3). Article 10 of [PS1] has two paragraphs. The extension in Article 10(1) is triggered only by omission of the Article 6(1)(h) information. Non-delivery is governed by [PS3] and national law (Section 4.5).

9.2 "A request under Article 7(3) ends the right on performance" — a request alone does not. The right is lost only on full performance, with prior express consent and acknowledgement (Article 16(a) of [PS1]); partial performance leaves the right intact and triggers proportionate payment under Article 14(3).

9.3 "12 months from the trigger day" as a description of Article 10(1) — the 12 months run from the END of the initial withdrawal period. Only the Article 10(2) window runs from the trigger day.

9.4 The brief does not mention Article 9(1a) (30 days). It must be checked for every target market.

9.5 The brief treats the periods as uniform across Member States. The Directive is a floor in places and leaves day-counting and non-working-day treatment to national law. The draft above therefore states the baseline and flags the national points rather than resolving them.
