# ECHR Article 6 § 2 — The Presumption of Innocence: Verbatim Text, Full Citation and Verification Note

**Status:** Draft training material for review by a qualified attorney. Not legal advice. Every proposition of law below is tied to a primary source named in full; propositions drawn from secondary ECHR publications are labelled as such.

**Jurisdiction:** Council of Europe member States that are High Contracting Parties to the European Convention on Human Rights, as applied and interpreted by the European Court of Human Rights. Nothing here asserts that the presumption of innocence in this form binds courts outside that system; domestic-law equivalents must be checked separately in each jurisdiction.

---

## 1. The answer — verbatim text

**Article 6 § 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, in the text presented as amended through Protocol No. 15:**

> “2. Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law.”

For a slide box without the paragraph number:

> “Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law.”

**Word-level accuracy points for the slide designer.** The sentence contains no internal punctuation and no semicolon; it ends with a single full stop. The operative words are “**proved**” (not “proven”), “**presumed innocent**” (not “presumed to be innocent”), and “**according to law**” (not “in accordance with law”, not “by law”). Variants of all three appear routinely in secondary summaries; any of them appearing in the module is a misquotation and should be corrected against the source at § 3 below.

**Answer to the “what presumption” question, stated plainly:** the presumption of innocence — Article 6 § 2 ECHR. It is a presumption operating in favour of “everyone charged with a criminal offence”, and it runs “until proved guilty according to law”.

---

## 2. Citation in full (use this form in the module's source note)

- **Convention:** Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (European Convention on Human Rights), Rome, 4 November 1950, **ETS No. 5**, Article 6 § 2, as amended by Protocol No. 11 (ETS No. 155), Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) and Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213), consolidated English text published by the Council of Europe / European Court of Human Rights under the title *“European Convention on Human Rights, as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15, supplemented by Protocols Nos. 1, 4, 6, 7, 12, 13 and 16”*.
- **Amending instrument relied on for the “as amended through Protocol No. 15” constraint:** Protocol No. 15 amending the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, **CETS No. 213**, entered into force **1 August 2021**.
- **Court publication used for the interpretive gloss in § 6:** European Court of Human Rights, *Guide on Article 6 of the Convention – Right to a fair trial (criminal limb)*, last update 28 February 2026, § 362 and the Article 6 quotation box (secondary source; it reproduces the Article 6 text and cites the case law).

---

## 3. Verification that the quoted text is the Protocol No. 15 version

The constraint is that the text be the one “presented as amended through Protocol No. 15”. That is verified from the document's own front matter, quoted verbatim:

> “The text of the Convention is presented as amended by the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021 and of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) as from its entry into force on 1 June 2010.”

Three further checks, each of which the reviewing attorney can repeat in under a minute:

1. **The cover title itself carries the constraint.** The consolidated English text is titled “as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15”.
2. **Amendments are footnoted where they occur, and Article 6 has no such footnote.** In the same consolidated text, provisions touched by Protocol No. 15 carry an express footnote — for example, the preamble sentence on subsidiarity and the margin of appreciation ends with footnote “1”, which reads: *“Text amended in accordance with the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021.”* Article 6 § 2 carries no equivalent footnote in either consolidated version consulted. The absence is therefore meaningful, not an omission.
3. **Do not misread the page numbers.** In the ECHR PDF the digits “10 11” appear between Article 6 § 2 and § 3. Those are the printed page numbers of the booklet, not footnote markers and not amendment notes. Flagging this because it is an easy and embarrassing error to propagate into a slide.

**Limit of this verification, stated honestly:** the negative proposition “Protocol No. 15 did not amend Article 6 § 2” is supported here by the consolidated text's own footnote convention plus the absence of any footnote at Article 6. The belt-and-braces check is the exhaustive list of amended provisions in **Protocol No. 15, Article 1 (CETS No. 213)**. The text of CETS No. 213, Article 1 was not among the materials retrieved for this draft, so that cross-check is listed as a verification step in § 9 rather than asserted. It does not affect the answer: whatever else Protocol No. 15 changed, the operative sentence in § 1 is what the Protocol No. 15 consolidated text prints at Article 6 § 2.

---

## 4. Scope of what the quoted sentence itself says

The text is one sentence and it says three things: (i) the addressee is “everyone charged with a criminal offence”; (ii) the presumption is that such a person is “innocent”; (iii) it operates “until proved guilty according to law”. The sentence does **not** expressly state who bears the burden of proof, what standard of proof applies, or that silence is protected. Those propositions come from the Court's case law, not from the words of Article 6 § 2, and the module should attribute them accordingly (see § 6).

Related but distinct provisions in the same Article, for accurate cross-referencing:

> “1. In the determination of his civil rights and obligations or of any criminal charge against him, everyone is entitled to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. […]”
>
> “3. Everyone charged with a criminal offence has the following minimum rights: (a) to be informed promptly, in a language which he understands and in detail, of the nature and cause of the accusation against him; (b) to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence; (c) to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing or, if he has not sufficient means to pay for legal assistance, to be given it free when the interests of justice so require; (d) to examine or have examined witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him; (e) to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in court.”

---

## 5. Language versions

The English text in § 1 is the English authentic version as consolidated by the Council of Europe. The Convention was concluded in English and French, both texts equally authentic (Convention, concluding formula, Rome, 4 November 1950). The French rendering of Article 6 § 2, for a bilingual module, is:

> « 2. Toute personne accusée d'une infraction est présumée innocente jusqu'à ce que sa culpabilité ait été légalement établie. »

**Verification flag:** the French sentence above is reproduced here for the drafter's convenience and must be checked character-for-character against the ECHR's French consolidated version before it is published in any bilingual material. The English text in § 1 is the verified one; do not treat the two as equally verified on the strength of this draft. If the module is delivered in another official language of a member State, quote from that State's official translation only with a note identifying the translator and the date, and keep the English authentic text alongside it.

---

## 6. Case-law gloss — clearly labelled as gloss

The following propositions come from the European Court of Human Rights and are cited to the Court's own *Guide on Article 6 (criminal limb)*, which in turn cites the judgments. They should appear in the module as “what the Court has held”, never as “what Article 6 § 2 says”.

- **Core content of the presumption.** “Paragraph 2 of Article 6 embodies the principle of the presumption of innocence. It requires, inter alia, that: (1) when carrying out their duties, the members of a court should not start with the preconceived idea that the accused has committed the offence charged; (2) the burden of proof is on the prosecution, and (3) any doubt should benefit the accused.” — *Guide on Article 6 (criminal limb)*, § 362, citing **Barberà, Messegué and Jabardo v. Spain, 6 December 1988, § 77, Series A no. 146**.
- **Presumptions of fact or law are not prohibited in principle.** “A person's right in a criminal case to be presumed innocent and to require the prosecution to bear the onus of proving the allegations against him or her is not absolute, since presumptions of fact or of law operate in every criminal-law system and are not prohibited in principle by the Convention […]” — *Guide on Article 6 (criminal limb)*. The underlying authority is **Salabiaku v. France, 7 October 1988, § 28, Series A no. 141-A**; confirm the pin cite against HUDOC before it goes on a slide, as the Guide passage as retrieved does not print the citation.
- **Who counts as “charged”.** The Court has treated as “charged with a criminal offence”, and thus within Article 6 protection, a person arrested on suspicion of a criminal offence, a suspect questioned about his involvement in acts constituting a criminal offence, and a person questioned about suspected involvement irrespective of being formally treated as a witness, as well as a person formally charged under domestic procedure — *Guide on Article 6 (criminal limb)*, citing *inter alia* **Heaney and McGuinness v. Ireland, no. 34720/97, § 42, ECHR 2000-XII** and **Deweer v. Belgium, 27 February 1980, §§ 41–47, Series A no. 35**. Application numbers and report citations for the remaining cases listed in the Guide should be completed from HUDOC before publication.
- **The guarantee outlives the trial.** The presumption also protects persons acquitted or whose proceedings were discontinued from being treated by public officials and authorities as though they were in fact guilty — *Guide on Article 6 (criminal limb)*. It may be infringed not only by a judge or court but also by other public authorities — same source.

**Do-not-say list for the trainer** (each of these overstates the text):

1. Do not say Article 6 § 2 “places the burden of proof on the prosecution” as a matter of the text — that is the *Barberà* gloss.
2. Do not say Article 6 § 2 contains a right to silence or a privilege against self-incrimination — those are separate guarantees developed in the case law and should be cited separately.
3. Do not say the presumption is absolute — the Guide expressly records that it is not, because presumptions of fact or law are not prohibited in principle.
4. Do not present the sentence as a rule of evidence binding on non-criminal proceedings without checking the civil limb (Article 6 § 1) and the relevant case law.
5. Do not attribute the quoted words to Protocol No. 15, or describe them as “new” or “amended” — they are the unchanged Article 6 § 2 wording carried into the Protocol No. 15 consolidated text.

---

## 7. Jurisdictional framing for the module

The Convention obligation is territorial and jurisdictional in scope. Article 1, as amended by Protocol No. 15, reads:

> “The High Contracting Parties shall secure to everyone within their jurisdiction the rights and freedoms defined in Section I of this Convention.”

with the footnote: *“Text amended in accordance with the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021.”* The module should therefore say that Article 6 § 2 binds Council of Europe member States Parties to the Convention and is interpreted by the European Court of Human Rights, and should not assume the same formulation governs in non-member jurisdictions or in domestic systems that protect the presumption by constitutional or statutory provision in different words.

---

## 8. Drop-in slide text (subject to attorney sign-off)

**Heading:** The presumption of innocence — Article 6 § 2 ECHR

**Verbatim box (quote exactly, in quotation marks, with the citation beneath):**
“Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law.”
*Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (ETS No. 5), Art. 6 § 2, as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15 (Protocol No. 15, CETS No. 213, in force 1 August 2021).*

**Gloss box (labelled “Court's interpretation, not the text”):** The European Court of Human Rights reads Article 6 § 2 as requiring that judges approach a case without a preconceived view of guilt, that the prosecution bear the burden of proof, and that doubt benefit the accused — *Barberà, Messegué and Jabardo v. Spain*, 6 December 1988, § 77, Series A no. 146.

---

## 9. Verification checklist before publication

1. Re-pull the ECHR consolidated English text and confirm the sentence in § 1 character-for-character, including “proved” and “according to law”.
2. Open **Protocol No. 15, Article 1 (CETS No. 213)** and confirm that Article 6 does not appear in the list of amended provisions — this converts the footnote-convention inference in § 3 into a direct citation.
3. Verify the French text in § 5 against the ECHR's French consolidated version.
4. Confirm the *Salabiaku* and remaining case citations in § 6 against HUDOC, completing application numbers and report citations.
5. Confirm the module's audience jurisdiction and, if it is a single member State, add the domestic provision implementing Article 6 § 2 with its own citation.
6. Re-check the “do-not-say” list against the final slide deck.

---

MEMORANDUM — COMBINED INTERVAL FROM SERVICE OF COMPLAINT TO SCHEDULING CONFERENCE, FTC PART 3 (SINGLE RESPONDENT)

Jurisdiction / procedure: Federal administrative adjudication before the Federal Trade Commission under 16 C.F.R. Part 3 (Rules of Practice for Adjudicative Proceedings), as in force on 2026-11-21. Not a court proceeding; the FTC's own rules supply the periods.

DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW — NOT LEGAL ADVICE.

1. QUESTION PRESENTED
In a single-respondent FTC Part 3 adjudication governed by the version of Part 3 in force on 2026-11-21, where the respondent uses the entire answer period and the ALJ then uses the entire period allowed after the answer to hold the scheduling conference, what is the combined interval from service of the complaint to the conference, using only those two periods?

2. ANSWER
24 days.

3. GOVERNING AUTHORITY (quoted verbatim; primary sources cited in full)

(A) Answer period — 16 C.F.R. § 3.12(a) (2026): "A respondent shall file an answer within 14 days after being served with the complaint."
Source: Code of Federal Regulations, Title 16 (Commercial Practices), Chapter I, Subchapter A, Part 3, § 3.12(a), 2026 edition, U.S. Government Publishing Office, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title16-vol1/xml/CFR-2026-title16-vol1-part3.xml (text also at https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-3). Stated period: 14 days, running from service of the complaint.

(B) Conference period — 16 C.F.R. § 3.21(b) (2026): "Not later than 10 days after the answer is filed by the last answering respondent, the Administrative Law Judge shall hold a scheduling conference."
Source: 16 C.F.R. § 3.21(b) (2026), https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/part-3/section-3.21 and https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title16-vol1/xml/CFR-2026-title16-vol1-part3.xml. Stated period: 10 days, running from the filing of the answer.

(C) Corroboration in Commission pleading practice: the Commission's Part 3 administrative complaint in In re Microsoft Corp./Activision Blizzard, Inc., FTC Docket No. 9412 (public version), states: "The Administrative Law Judge shall hold a prehearing scheduling conference not later than ten (10) days after the Respondents file their answers" and "the opportunity is afforded you to file with the Commission an answer to this complaint on or before the fourteenth (14th) day after service of it upon you." Source: https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/D09412MicrosoftActivisionAdministrativeComplaintPublicVersionFinal.pdf. This confirms the two periods are 14 and 10 in the operative rule text; the rule, not the complaint form, controls.

4. COMPUTATION
Step 1 — Answer. Service of the complaint starts the § 3.12(a) clock. Full use of the period places the answer on the 14th day after service.
Step 2 — Conference. The § 3.21(b) clock starts on filing of the answer. Because there is one respondent, the sole respondent is the "last answering respondent"; no other answer can extend the trigger. Full use of the period places the conference on the 10th day after the answer.
Step 3 — Combine (sequential, not concurrent). 14 days + 10 days = 24 days after service.

Worked timeline (day of service excluded, the ordinary convention):
- Day 0 — complaint served.
- Day 14 — answer filed (last day of § 3.12(a) period).
- Day 24 — scheduling conference held (last day of § 3.21(b) period).
- Combined interval: 24 days.

5. DAY-COUNTING CONVENTION — WHAT IT DOES AND DOES NOT CHANGE
The two periods are stated in calendar days, not business days; neither § 3.12(a) nor § 3.21(b) says "business days." The 24-day total is the sum of the two stated periods and is invariant to the endpoint convention: counting the day of service as day 1 rather than day 0 shifts the calendar date of each step by one day but does not change 14 + 10 = 24. What the convention does affect is the calendar date on which the 24th day falls. If that date is a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday, a computation-of-time provision in Part 3 (16 C.F.R. § 3.7) would in the ordinary course roll the deadline to the next business day, producing an actual interval of 25 or 26 days. That roll is an application of a separate rule, not one of the two stated periods, and is therefore outside the figure requested. I did not retrieve the verified text of § 3.7 in this pass and do not quote or rely on it; it should be confirmed against the 2026 edition before any calendar date is fixed. The 24-day figure does not depend on it.

6. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS ON THE FIGURE
(a) 24 days is a maximum under full use of both periods, not a typical or required timeline. If the respondent answers early, the § 3.21(b) trigger moves earlier and the interval shortens.
(b) Single respondent: no consolidation and no co-respondent whose later answer would reset the "last answering respondent" trigger.
(c) No extensions (16 C.F.R. § 3.21(c)(2) allows the ALJ, on good cause, to extend deadlines in the scheduling order), no motions to extend the answer, no amended complaint, no stay or tolling (compare the tolling provision for dispositive motions at 16 C.F.R. § 3.24(d)).
(d) Excluded by the "only those two periods" instruction, though they occur inside the same window: the § 3.21(a) meet-and-confer (no later than 5 days after the answers) and the § 3.21(c)(1) prehearing scheduling order (no later than 2 days after the conference). Adding them would overstate the requested figure.
(e) Service method: § 3.12(a) runs from service. If service was by a method that Part 3 treats as adding days, the answer date moves; the request fixes the answer period at its stated length, so no add-on is applied here.
(f) The date of the evidentiary hearing (5 months or 8 months from the complaint under 16 C.F.R. § 3.11(b)(4)) is unrelated to this calculation and does not constrain it.

7. CONCLUSION
Using only the two stated periods in 16 C.F.R. Part 3 as in force on 2026-11-21 — 14 days for the answer (§ 3.12(a)) and 10 days after the answer for the scheduling conference (§ 3.21(b)) — the combined interval from service of the complaint to the conference is 24 days.
cautions: The recompute vote compared nothing, so no figure in this answer was recomputed independently.
The answer gives 24 days for ask 1, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

THRESHOLD MARGIN CALCULATION — ARTICLE 1(2)(a)–(b), COUNCIL REGULATION (EC) No 139/2004
Jurisdiction: European Union. These thresholds are specific to the EU merger control regime; they say nothing about any national merger control regime or any other jurisdiction.

1. SCOPE AND INSTRUCTION
This memorandum does one thing: it states, for each of the three recorded turnover amounts, the arithmetical amount by which that amount exceeds the corresponding threshold in Article 1(2)(a) and (b) of Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004. It does not determine, and must not be read as determining, whether any concentration has a Community dimension. No such conclusion is drawn anywhere below (see §6).

2. THE RULE AND THE THRESHOLDS (primary source)
Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 of 20 January 2004 on the control of concentrations between undertakings (the EC Merger Regulation), OJ L 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1–22, Article 1(2), provides:

"2. A concentration has a Community dimension where:
(a) the combined aggregate worldwide turnover of all the undertakings concerned is more than EUR 5000 million; and
(b) the aggregate Community-wide turnover of each of at least two of the undertakings concerned is more than EUR 250 million,
unless each of the undertakings concerned achieves more than two-thirds of its aggregate Community-wide turnover within one and the same Member State."

Source: Regulation (EC) No 139/2004, Art. 1(2)(a)–(b), OJ L 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1; ELI http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/139/oj (text as published; the same wording appears in the English text at https://wipolex-res.wipo.int/edocs/lexdocs/laws/en/eu/eu104en.html).

Thresholds applied: (a) EUR 5,000 million, combined aggregate worldwide turnover of all undertakings concerned; (b) EUR 250 million, aggregate Community-wide turnover of each of at least two undertakings concerned.

Note the statutory comparator is "more than". Equality with the threshold does not satisfy it; every figure below is strictly above its threshold, so the margins are positive.

3. THE COMPUTATION
All amounts in EUR million, as recorded by the filing team, compared directly with the statutory figures. No currency conversion has been applied (all figures recorded in EUR).

Line 1 — Article 1(2)(a), combined aggregate worldwide turnover
  Recorded amount ......................... 5,400
  Threshold ............................... 5,000
  Excess (recorded − threshold) ........... 400
  Arithmetic .............................. 5,400 − 5,000 = 400; check 5,000 + 400 = 5,400

Line 2 — Article 1(2)(b), Community-wide turnover, undertaking 1
  Recorded amount ......................... 300
  Threshold ............................... 250
  Excess (recorded − threshold) ........... 50
  Arithmetic .............................. 300 − 250 = 50; check 250 + 50 = 300

Line 3 — Article 1(2)(b), Community-wide turnover, undertaking 2
  Recorded amount ......................... 275
  Threshold ............................... 250
  Excess (recorded − threshold) ........... 25
  Arithmetic .............................. 275 − 250 = 25; check 250 + 25 = 275

Summary of answers (EUR million):
  Combined worldwide turnover: exceeds EUR 5,000 million by EUR 400 million.
  Community-wide turnover, undertaking 1: exceeds EUR 250 million by EUR 50 million.
  Community-wide turnover, undertaking 2: exceeds EUR 250 million by EUR 25 million.

For reference only, the margins as a proportion of the threshold are 8.0% (400/5,000), 20.0% (50/250) and 10.0% (25/250). These percentages are descriptive; nothing in Article 1(2) turns on proportionality, only on the strict "more than" comparison.

4. ASSUMPTIONS ON WHICH THESE THREE FIGURES DEPEND (each is a point to confirm, not a finding)
(a) Threshold figures. The calculation uses the Article 1(2)(a)–(b) figures of EUR 5,000 million and EUR 250 million as they appear in the published text cited in §2. No amending or successor instrument was consulted; the figures should be re-verified against the consolidated version of Regulation 139/2004 in force on the date of the transaction. If either figure has changed, every margin above changes with it.
(b) Quality of the recorded amounts. The recorded amounts are taken as final turnover figures already calculated in accordance with Article 5 of Regulation 139/2004 — i.e. turnover of the undertakings concerned as aggregated under Article 5(4), net of intra-group and joint-venture sales as required by Article 5(5), and, where only parts of an undertaking are acquired, limited to the parts that are the subject of the concentration per Article 5(2) ("By way of derogation from paragraph 1, where the concentration consists of the acquisition of parts ... only the turnover relating to the parts which are the subject of the concentration shall be taken into account with regard to the seller or sellers."). Sources: Regulation (EC) No 139/2004, Art. 5(2), 5(4), 5(5). If the recorded figures are raw or provisional rather than Article 5-compliant, the margins must be recalculated after adjustment; a figure close to a threshold can move across it.
(c) Identity of the entities. The two Community-wide figures are assumed to correspond to two distinct undertakings concerned as that concept applies under the Regulation. Whether the recorded group perimeter matches the Article 5(4) aggregation perimeter is not verified here.
(d) Financial year and currency. The figures are assumed to relate to the same preceding financial year and to be expressed in euro, so that no conversion and no year-alignment adjustment is required. No exchange rate is applied.

5. WHAT THESE MARGINS DO AND DO NOT ESTABLISH
A positive margin means only that the recorded amount is greater than the statutory figure. It does not establish that the corresponding condition of Article 1(2) is legally satisfied, for at least four reasons that are outside this calculation: (i) Article 1(2) contains its own proviso — the two-thirds Member State rule — which is part of the operative test, not a separate defence; (ii) Article 1(2)(b) requires the condition to be met by "each of at least two" undertakings concerned, which depends on correctly identifying the undertakings concerned; (iii) Article 1(3) sets an alternative set of thresholds (EUR 2,500 million / EUR 100 million / EUR 25 million / EUR 100 million), which is not addressed here and on which no arithmetic is performed; and (iv) the referral mechanisms (Articles 4(5), 9 and 22) and the turnover rules of Article 5 are not applied here. Separately, the EUR 250 million figure that appears in Form CO point 3.5.2 is the EFTA-cooperation-case test for turnover in the territory of the EFTA States (Commission Regulation (EC) No 802/2004, Annex I (Form CO), points 3.3.1–3.3.3, 3.4 and 3.5.2, OJ L 133, 30.4.2004, p. 1, as amended) and is a different test from Article 1(2)(b); it is mentioned only so that it is not confused with the figure used above.

6. EXPRESS NON-DETERMINATION
No view is expressed, and none should be inferred, on whether the concentration has a Community dimension, whether Article 1(2) is satisfied or disapplied, whether the two-thirds proviso applies, whether Article 1(3) applies, or whether any notification, referral or filing obligation arises. The three figures in §3 are arithmetic differences and nothing more.

7. DEADLINES, NOTICE AND SERVICE
No deadline, notice period or service step is calculated or tracked here: the request supplies no trigger date (no signature, announcement, completion or notification date) and asks no timing question. If a trigger date is later supplied, the relevant periods would have to be counted under the provisions that create them (including Regulation 139/2004, Article 4(1) and the time-limit rules in Commission Regulation (EC) No 802/2004, Chapter III, including Article 24 on the definition of working days), and that would be a separate calculation.

8. SOURCES (full citations)
1. Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 of 20 January 2004 on the control of concentrations between undertakings (the EC Merger Regulation), OJ L 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1–22 — Article 1(2)(a)–(b) (thresholds and two-thirds proviso), Article 1(3) (alternative thresholds, referred to only to exclude), Article 5(2), 5(4), 5(5) (turnover calculation). ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/139/oj.
2. Commission Regulation (EC) No 802/2004 of 7 April 2004 implementing Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 on the control of concentrations between undertakings, OJ L 133, 30.4.2004, p. 1–39 (as amended) — Annex I (Form CO), points 2.4, 2.4.1, 3.3.1–3.3.3, 3.4, 3.5.2; Chapter III (time-limits) and Article 24 (definition of working days). ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/802/oj/eng.
3. English text of Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 reproduced at https://wipolex-res.wipo.int/edocs/lexdocs/laws/en/eu/eu104en.html (consulted for the Article 1(2) wording; the OJ text at source 1 is authoritative).

question: Y134
answer:
# MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW

**This is a draft work product for review by a qualified attorney. It is not legal advice and must not be relied on by a client in its unreviewed form.**

**Subject:** Directive 2011/83/EU, Article 3(4) optional exclusion for low-value off-premises contracts (Member State option exercised at the EUR 50 maximum) — (i) what total is used for the threshold where a consumer simultaneously concludes two contracts with related subjects for EUR 30 and EUR 25, and (ii) whether the exclusion covers that pair on that basis.

**Jurisdiction:** European Union (Directive level). The Member State whose transposition governs is not identified in the instruction; the EU-level answer is given in Parts A–E and the Member-State-dependent points are isolated in Part F. A rule that holds at Directive level is not assumed to hold identically in every national transposition.

---

## PART A — ANSWERS

### A.1 (Ask 1) Total used for the threshold: **EUR 55**

The two prices are **aggregated**: EUR 30 + EUR 25 = **EUR 55**. The EUR 50 threshold is not applied contract-by-contract where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer. The aggregation rule is stated in Recital 28 of Directive 2011/83/EU:

> “Where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer, the total cost thereof should be taken into account for the purpose of applying this threshold.”

### A.2 (Ask 2) Does the optional exclusion cover this pair on that basis: **No**

Article 3(4) of Directive 2011/83/EU permits a Member State to disapply the Directive only to off-premises contracts “for which the payment to be made by the consumer **does not exceed EUR 50**”. The relevant payment on the aggregation rule is **EUR 55**, which **exceeds** EUR 50 by EUR 5. The exclusion is therefore **unavailable for the pair**, and the consequence is not that one contract is excluded and the other is not — it is that the exclusion cannot be relied on at all, so **both** contracts remain within the Directive and within the national transposition, carrying the full Chapter III information and withdrawal regime.

**Direction of the test (worth stating expressly in any advice):** “does not exceed” means ≤ EUR 50. A pair totalling exactly EUR 50 would fall inside the exclusion. EUR 55 does not.

### A.3 Worked threshold table

| Unit of assessment | Payment | Cumulative total | Exceeds EUR 50? | Exclusion available? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contract 1 alone | EUR 30 | EUR 30 | No | Yes (if assessed alone) |
| Contract 2 alone | EUR 25 | EUR 25 | No | Yes (if assessed alone) |
| **Pair, aggregated (correct test)** | **EUR 30 + EUR 25** | **EUR 55** | **Yes** | **No** |

**Why the aggregation rule is outcome-determinative here.** Both legs are individually below the ceiling. Without aggregation, the trader would escape the Directive on **both** contracts; with aggregation, the trader escapes on **neither**. This is precisely the contract-splitting pattern the rule exists to defeat, and the pair should be advised on that footing.

---

## PART B — PRIMARY SOURCES RELIED ON (full citations)

**B.1 Directive 2011/83/EU.** Directive 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on consumer rights, amending Council Directive 93/13/EEC and Directive 1999/44/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Council Directive 85/577/EEC and Directive 97/7/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council, OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64–88; ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/83/oj (consolidated text consulted on EUR-Lex, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/83/oj).

Provisions relied on: Article 3(1), Article 3(4), Article 3(5), Article 4, Article 6(1)(e), Article 13(1), Article 15(1); Recital 28.

**B.2 European Commission guidance (persuasive, not binding).** European Commission, *Guidance on the interpretation and application of Directive 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council on consumer rights*, OJ C 525, 29.12.2021, p. 1 — section 1.8, “Possible exemption of low value off-premises contracts”. Copy consulted: Publications Office CELLAR, http://publications.europa.eu/resource/cellar/a5f87ef3-6849-11ec-9136-01aa75ed71a1.0006.03/DOC_1. **[Action for reviewing attorney: confirm the OJ C 525 pagination against the Official Journal before this citation is used in a filed document; the CELLAR URI is the copy actually consulted.]**

**B.3 Case law on interpretive method (cited for method, not for the aggregation rule itself — see C.6).**
- Case C-14/83 *Sabine von Colson and Elisabeth Kamann v Land Nordrhein-Westfalen* [1984] ECR 1891 (duty of conforming interpretation of national law implementing a directive).
- Case C-106/89 *Marleasing SA v La Comercial Internacional de Alimentación SA* [1990] ECR I-4135 (conforming interpretation extends to national law adopted to implement a directive and to pre-existing national law).
- Case C-322/88 *Salvatore Grimaldi v Fonds des maladies professionnelles* [1989] ECR 4407 (recommendations and guidance lack binding force but are persuasive interpretive material for national courts).
- Case C-162/97 *Criminal proceedings against Gunnar Nilsson and others* [1998] ECR I-7477, para. 54 (a preamble/recital has no binding legal force of its own and cannot be used to derogate from the operative provisions — cited here **against** the aggregation argument as well as for it; see C.5).

**B.4 National transposition.** Not identified in the instruction. See Part F for exactly what must be obtained and checked.

---

## PART C — ANALYSIS

### C.1 The two-limb structure of Article 3(4)

Article 3(4) provides, verbatim:

> “Member States may decide not to apply this Directive or not to maintain or introduce corresponding national provisions to off-premises contracts for which the payment to be made by the consumer does not exceed EUR 50. Member States may define a lower value in their national legislation.”

Two features matter.

1. **It is a Member State option, not a trader defence arising automatically.** The exclusion operates only if, and to the extent that, the Member State has exercised it. The instruction fixes the premise that the Member State has exercised it at the EUR 50 maximum, so the ceiling to be applied is EUR 50 and no lower national figure applies.
2. **It is a total disapplication, not a partial one.** The text reads “not to apply **this Directive**”, not “not to apply the withdrawal right”. If the exclusion applies, the Directive as a whole does not apply to the contract and the consumer’s position is governed by national general law. If it does not apply, the Directive applies in full. There is no intermediate state. This matters to how the answer is framed: the question “does the exclusion cover the pair” is a scope question, not a question about which individual rights survive.

### C.2 The aggregation rule

Recital 28, verbatim:

> “In order to avoid administrative burden being placed on traders, Member States may decide not to apply this Directive where goods or services of a minor value are sold off-premises. The monetary threshold should be established at a sufficiently low level as to exclude only purchases of small significance. Member States should be allowed to define this value in their national legislation provided that it does not exceed EUR 50. **Where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer, the total cost thereof should be taken into account for the purpose of applying this threshold.**”

The Commission’s guidance reads the same rule and identifies its anti-circumvention purpose in terms, verbatim:

> “Article 3(4) allows Member States not to apply the Directive to off-premises contracts, for which the payment to be made by the consumer does not exceed EUR 50 or a lower value as defined under national law. If a Member State chooses to use this regulatory choice, there is a risk that the Directive gets circumvented by traders who may decide to artificially split a single contract above the set threshold into several contracts. As explained in Recital 28: ‘[…] Where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer, the total cost thereof should be taken into account for the purpose of applying this threshold.’ This principle would apply to: — For example, selling each book of a trilogy under three separate contracts or selling a pair of earrings under two separate contracts at the same time.”

The two worked examples — a trilogy split into three book contracts, and a pair of earrings split into two contracts — are the closest guidance-level analogy to a pair of related contracts priced at EUR 30 and EUR 25 concluded at the same time. The guidance also confirms the measurement rule for continuing contracts: “For long-term contracts (subscriptions), the relevant amount for the application of this exception is the total amount that the consumer commits to pay when concluding the contract. i.e. the total amount of monthly instalments or charges over the agreed contractual period, including any ‘free’ periods.” That is not needed on the assumed facts (single payments), but it should be checked if either contract has a recurring element.

### C.3 The operative test to be applied

Two cumulative conditions, both drawn from the recital text:

**(a) “concluded at the same time”.** The instruction assumes simultaneity (“simultaneously concludes … at the same time in the course of a single commercial transaction”). Treat as satisfied on the assumed facts. If it were contested, the relevant evidence is the timing of offer and acceptance, whether a single visit/occasion produced both, and whether the trader presented them as one transaction.

**(b) “contracts with related subjects”.** The Directive does not define this phrase in Article 2. It is not a term of art with a settled autonomous meaning. The Commission’s examples (the trilogy; the earrings) indicate that the relation is one of shared commercial object — goods or services forming a set, collection or single economic purchase, or obligations that are interdependent. Indicators an attorney should test on the file: same trader; same occasion and same place; a single commercial purpose from the consumer’s standpoint; interdependence of the obligations (performance of one is pointless or impaired without the other); presentation as a package or with cross-referenced terms; a single payment, single delivery or single invoice; and whether the consumer would reasonably have understood the transaction as one purchase.

On the instruction’s own characterisation (“two contracts with related subjects”), condition (b) is treated as given. **This is the single factual point on which the whole answer pivots** — if the two contracts are genuinely unrelated (independent purchases that happened to be made at the same time from the same trader), aggregation does not apply, each contract is assessed at EUR 30 and EUR 25 respectively, both fall below EUR 50, and the exclusion covers both. That is the opposite result, and the reviewing attorney should not let the characterisation pass unexamined.

### C.4 Application to the facts

- Condition (a): satisfied (assumed simultaneity).
- Condition (b): satisfied (instruction characterises the contracts as with related subjects; the trilogy/earrings analogies in the Commission guidance support it).
- Therefore the threshold is tested on the **total cost**: EUR 30 + EUR 25 = **EUR 55**.
- EUR 55 > EUR 50. The condition in Article 3(4) — payment “does not exceed EUR 50” — is **not** met.
- **The optional exclusion does not cover the pair.**

### C.5 Consequence of the exclusion not applying

Because Article 3(4) is an all-or-nothing disapplication (C.1), the failure of the exclusion means the Directive and its national transposition apply to **both** contracts, including:

- the pre-contractual information duties in Article 6, including the total price inclusive of taxes and additional charges under Article 6(1)(e);
- the withdrawal regime in Articles 9 to 16 (the 14-day period and its consequences), subject to any Article 16 exception that independently applies on the facts;
- Article 13(1) reimbursement: “The trader shall reimburse all payments received from the consumer, including, if applicable, the costs of delivery without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days from the day on which he is informed of the consumer’s decision to withdraw from the contract in accordance with Article 11.”
- **A practical point the file should be checked for:** if one of the two contracts is ancillary to the other (credit, insurance, installation, extended warranty), Article 15(1) provides that on withdrawal from the main distance or off-premises contract “any ancillary contracts shall be automatically terminated, without any costs for the consumer, except as provided for in Article 13(2) and in Article 14 of this Directive.” On a related-subjects pair this is a live possibility and materially changes the remedy.

### C.6 Counter-arguments and where the authority is thin

Stated plainly, because the reviewing attorney needs to know the weak joints.

**(i) The aggregation rule is in a recital, not in the operative text.** Article 3(4) contains no aggregation sentence. A trader could argue that Article 3(4) as enacted tests “the payment to be made by the consumer” under each contract, and that Recital 28 cannot supply a condition absent from the operative provision. The counter is that recitals are a recognised interpretive aid and that Article 3(4) must be read in the light of the objective Recital 28 articulates (excluding only “purchases of small significance” and preventing circumvention by splitting). The counter-counter is *Nilsson* (C-162/97, para. 54): a preamble has no binding force and cannot be relied on to derogate from the operative provisions. **This is a genuine argument and the answer is not free from doubt at Directive level.** In practice it is resolved less by EU-law argument than by the national transposition, which in most Member States that used the option reproduces the aggregation rule (Part F).

**(ii) No CJEU judgment on the aggregation rule was located.** The instruction’s research returned the Directive text, the Commission guidance and national implementing material, but no Court of Justice ruling construing “contracts with related subjects” or the aggregation mechanism. The authority at EU level is therefore a recital plus non-binding Commission guidance. The guidance is expressly persuasive only (*Grimaldi*, C-322/88). **Do not present the aggregation rule to a court as settled CJEU doctrine; present it as the Directive’s stated rule, reinforced by effet utile and by the national transposition.**

**(iii) The national transposition is unidentified.** This is the largest gap. If the Member State’s implementing provision reproduces the aggregation sentence, the answer is straightforward at national level and the Recital 28 debate is academic. If the implementing provision is silent, the consumer’s route is conforming interpretation (*von Colson*, C-14/83; *Marleasing*, C-106/89) — reading the national provision in the light of Article 3(4) and Recital 28 — which is a strong but not guaranteed route, and which cannot be used to interpret national law *contra legem*. See Part F.

**(iv) National general contract law is expressly preserved.** Article 3(5): “This Directive shall not affect national general contract law such as the rules on the validity, formation or effect of a contract, in so far as general contract law aspects are not regulated in this Directive.” Whether the two contracts form a single indivisible transaction, or whether splitting them is an abuse of right or a simulation, is a question of national civil law and may independently reinforce (or complicate) the Recital 28 analysis. It is not displaced by the Directive, and it should be pleaded alongside rather than instead of the aggregation argument.

**(v) Level of harmonisation.** Article 4 forbids Member States from maintaining or introducing divergent provisions “unless otherwise provided for in this Directive”. Article 3(4) is such an “otherwise provided for”. This confirms that the exclusion’s scope is fixed by the Directive’s terms and is not open to a Member State to widen by, for example, permitting per-contract assessment without aggregation — a further support for reading Article 3(4) subject to Recital 28.

### C.7 Measurement of “the payment to be made by the consumer”

Article 3(4) refers to “the payment to be made by the consumer”, not to “the price”; Recital 28 refers to “the total cost thereof”. Both formulations point to the total amount payable rather than a net figure. The instruction assumes the EUR 30 and EUR 25 figures are inclusive of any relevant charges for threshold purposes; that assumption is adopted. If it is wrong, the figures must be restated on a total-cost basis before the threshold is applied — delivery, booking and ancillary charges that the consumer must pay all count.

---

## PART D — ASSUMPTIONS (each to be confirmed, not treated as fact)

1. The Member State validly exercised the Article 3(4) option and set the exclusion at the EUR 50 maximum (not a lower figure).
2. The two contracts were concluded at the same time in the course of a single commercial transaction.
3. The contracts are “with related subjects” within the meaning of Recital 28.
4. The EUR 30 and EUR 25 figures are the total payments to be made by the consumer, inclusive of taxes and any additional charges.
5. Both contracts are off-premises contracts within Article 2(8) and neither falls within an Article 3(3) exclusion or an Article 16 exception on grounds independent of value.
6. Both amounts are denominated in euro; no currency conversion is required.
7. The contracts were concluded at a time when the transposing law in force included the option.

If assumption 3 fails, the answer to Ask 2 reverses (see C.3). If assumption 1 fails because the national figure is lower than EUR 50, the answer to Ask 2 does not change (a lower ceiling is exceeded a fortiori by EUR 55), though the analysis must cite the correct national figure.

---

## PART E — VERIFICATION CHECKLIST BEFORE THIS DRAFT IS USED

1. Obtain and quote the exact national implementing provision corresponding to Article 3(4), in the version in force at the date of conclusion.
2. Confirm whether that provision contains the aggregation sentence, and quote it verbatim if so.
3. Identify any national case law on contract-splitting or on “related subjects”/“related subject matter”.
4. Confirm the national threshold figure (EUR 50 or lower) and that it is not index-linked.
5. Confirm the contracts are off-premises contracts and that no Article 3(3) or Article 16 exclusion applies independently.
6. Confirm the total-cost figures (taxes and charges included).
7. Confirm the date of conclusion against the transposition’s entry into force.
8. Confirm the OJ citation of the Commission guidance (B.2).
9. Check whether either contract is ancillary to the other for Article 15(1) purposes.

---

## PART F — WHAT IS MEMBER-STATE-DEPENDENT (and what is not)

The following **do not** depend on the Member State: the arithmetic (EUR 30 + EUR 25 = EUR 55); the fact that EUR 55 exceeds EUR 50; the text of Article 3(4) and Recital 28; and the conclusion that, on the Directive’s own stated rule, the exclusion is unavailable for the pair.

The following **do** depend on the Member State and must be confirmed before advice is given:

- **The exact wording of the transposition.** Whether the aggregation sentence was carried into binding national law, and in what terms.
- **The legal test for “related subjects” in that jurisdiction.** No settled autonomous EU meaning exists (C.3); national courts may have supplied criteria.
- **The interaction with national general contract law** (Article 3(5)) — indivisibility, simulation, abuse of right, and any national rule against contract-splitting.
- **Currency conversion**, if either contract is not in euro; the Directive fixes EUR 50 and does not itself prescribe a conversion method.
- **Remedies and consequences** of the Directive applying — procedural and remedial detail is national.

If the transposition is silent on aggregation, the argument to run is: Article 3(4) must be construed in the light of Recital 28 and of the anti-circumvention objective it states; Article 4 precludes a divergent national widening of the exclusion; and the national provision must be interpreted conformably (*von Colson*, C-14/83; *Marleasing*, C-106/89). Flag the *Nilsson* limitation (C.6(i)) candidly in any advice.

answer:
DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

MEMORANDUM

TO: Supervising Attorney (manual revision)
FROM: Legal Research
RE: Status of the "Appendix of Forms" to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure under the rules as amended to December 1, 2025; effective date of the change; consequences for a 2014 litigation manual
JURISDICTION: United States — procedure in the U.S. district courts under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (Fed. R. Civ. P. 1). State-court procedural analogues are outside this memo; a rule stated here for the federal courts is not assumed to hold in any state.

=====================================================================
I. QUESTIONS PRESENTED
=====================================================================

1. [Constraint] Whether the analysis below is stated against the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure as amended to December 1, 2025.
2. What is the status, in those rules, of the Appendix of Forms to which a 2014 litigation manual still directs users?
3. When did that change take effect?

=====================================================================
II. SHORT ANSWERS
=====================================================================

1. Yes — every statement below is taken from the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure as amended to and including December 1, 2025 (Judicial Conference of the United States, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Foreword, Dec. 1, 2025).

2. ABROGATED. The Appendix of Forms is no longer a component of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. It was not renamed, suspended, relocated into the rule text, or replaced in place; it was abrogated in its entirety, together with Rule 84 — the rule that had given the forms operative effect. The rules now carry the abrogation parenthetical in the place where the Appendix stood: "XII. APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" and "Rule 84. [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]"

3. DECEMBER 1, 2015 (2015-12-01). The amendments were adopted by the Supreme Court by order dated April 29, 2015, transmitted to Congress by the Chief Justice the same day (575 U.S. 1055; Cong. Rec., vol. 161, pt. 5, p. 6139, Ex. Comm. 1373; H. Doc. 114-33), and became effective December 1, 2015 under the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. §§ 2072, 2074.

=====================================================================
III. GOVERNING AUTHORITY (full citations)
=====================================================================

Primary:

1. Order of the Supreme Court of the United States, April 29, 2015, adopting amendments to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, 575 U.S. 1055 (2015); transmitted to Congress by the Chief Justice April 29, 2015; Cong. Rec., vol. 161, pt. 5, p. 6139, Ex. Comm. 1373; H. Doc. 114-33. [Citation as given in the official pamphlet's historical note; the order's text was not in the materials reviewed — see § VII.]

2. Fed. R. Civ. P. 84 (abrogated Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).

3. Appendix of Forms, Fed. R. Civ. P., Title XII (abrogated Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).

4. 28 U.S.C. § 2072 (Rules Enabling Act — power to prescribe rules of procedure; rules "shall not abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right").

5. 28 U.S.C. § 2074 (congressional review; transmittal not later than May 1 of the year in which a rule is to take effect; rule takes effect no earlier than December 1 of that year unless otherwise provided by law).

6. Fed. R. Civ. P. 86(a) (Effective Dates — rules and amendments take effect at the time specified by the Supreme Court, subject to 28 U.S.C. § 2074).

7. Fed. R. Civ. P. 83 (Rules by District Courts; Judge's Directives) — governs local rules and local forms, the remaining source of court-specific form requirements.

8. Judicial Conference of the United States, Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (as amended to December 1, 2025), Foreword (Dec. 1, 2025) and Historical Note, https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23; sha256 bd8705fc038d).

9. Federal Judicial Center, Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure 2015—Civil Rules Redline (Dec. 1, 2015), https://www.fjc.gov/content/309299/amendments-federal-rules-practice-and-procedure-2015-civil-rules-redline (fetched 2026-11-23; sha256 7d0b770c9abc).

10. Federal Judicial Center, Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure 2015—Transmittal to Congress (Apr. 29, 2015), https://www.fjc.gov/content/309296/rules-amendments-2015-congress-transmittal (fetched 2026-11-23; sha256 6d90fc6fa153).

Secondary / corroborative only:

11. Cornell Legal Information Institute, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (as amended to December 1, 2025), https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp (fetched 2026-11-23; sha256 803b4574ea1a). Used solely to corroborate the abrogation parentheticals; not relied on as authority.

=====================================================================
IV. ANALYSIS
=====================================================================

A. What the Appendix of Forms was, and what it did

Since the original rules took effect on September 16, 1938, the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure carried an Appendix of Forms — simplified model pleadings and process papers appended to the rules themselves as Title XII. The forms were given operative effect by Rule 84. As restyled effective December 1, 2007, the Appendix contained Forms 1 through 82: the 2007 restyling converted the original Forms 1 through 35 into restyled Forms 1 through 82. Judicial Conference, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Historical Note (as amended to Dec. 1, 2025) ("Forms 1 through 35 were amended to become restyled Forms 1 through 82").

[Verification flag: former Rule 84 as restyled in 2007 read, in substance, that "[t]he forms in the Appendix suffice under these rules and illustrate the simplicity and brevity that these rules contemplate." That language is NOT in the December 1, 2025 pamphlet (which carries only the abrogation parenthetical), so it must be confirmed against a 2014 print of the Rules before it is quoted in any published annotation. See § VII, item 1.]

B. The 2015 amendment: two distinct abrogations

The 2015 package did two separate things that are frequently conflated:

(i) it abrogated Rule 84; and
(ii) it abrogated the Appendix of Forms (Forms 1 through 82).

Both are stated in the official pamphlet's historical note, verbatim: "Additional amendments were adopted by the Court by order dated April 29, 2015, transmitted to Congress by the Chief Justice on the same day (575 U.S. 1055; Cong. Rec., vol. 161, pt. 5, p. 6139, Ex. Comm. 1373; H. Doc. 114-33), and became effective December 1, 2015. The amendments affected Rules 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, and 55, abrogated Rule 84, and abrogated the Appendix of Forms (Forms 1 through 82)." (Judicial Conference, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Historical Note (as amended to Dec. 1, 2025).)

The Federal Judicial Center states the same in its own words: "Amendments to the following Federal Rules of Civil Procedure became effective on December 1, 2015: 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, and 55. Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms were abrogated." (FJC, 2015—Civil Rules Redline.) And in the transmittal package: "Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 84 and the Appendix of Forms were abrogated." (FJC, 2015—Transmittal to Congress.)

The distinction matters practically: abrogating the Appendix alone would have removed the forms while leaving Rule 84's safe harbor pointing at nothing; abrogating Rule 84 alone would have left forms with no rule-based effect. The 2015 package did both, so neither the forms nor the safe harbor survives.

C. Effective-date mechanics

Under 28 U.S.C. § 2074, a rule prescribed under § 2072 must be transmitted to Congress not later than May 1 of the year in which it is to become effective, and takes effect no earlier than December 1 of that year unless Congress provides otherwise. Rule 86(a) confirms that the rules and amendments "take effect at the time specified by the Supreme Court, subject to 28 U.S.C. § 2074."

The timeline is therefore:
- April 29, 2015 — Supreme Court order adopting the amendments; transmission to Congress by the Chief Justice the same day (within the May 1 window).
- December 1, 2015 — effective date, the earliest date § 2074 permits for a 2015 transmittal.

No statute deferring, modifying, or rejecting the 2015 package appears in the materials reviewed, and the official 2025 pamphlet and the FJC both record December 1, 2015 as the operative date. If the file requires negative confirmation of congressional action, that check is a search of the Statutes at Large / Congress.gov for 2015 legislation under § 2074; it is not a gap in the answer, only a belt-and-braces step.

D. Status as of December 1, 2025 — no resurrection

The rules as amended to December 1, 2025 contain no Appendix of Forms. The current official text shows the abrogation in place, at both locations:
- "Rule 84. [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" (Judicial Conference, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Title XI (as amended to Dec. 1, 2025).)
- "XII. APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" (same; corroborated at Cornell LII, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure index (as amended to Dec. 1, 2025), which lists "Rule 84. Abrogated, eff. Dec. 1, 2015" and "XII. APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]")

Nothing between 2015 and 2025 re-established the Appendix; the 2025 pamphlet continues to carry the 2015 parentheticals, and Title XIII (Supplemental Rules for Admiralty or Maritime Claims and Asset Forfeiture Actions) follows directly.

One nuance the manual must not blur: forms as a category did not disappear. The Foreword to the December 1, 2025 pamphlet still describes the document as containing "the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure together with forms, as amended to December 1, 2025." What disappeared is the Appendix of Forms as a titled component of the Rules and Rule 84's statement that those forms "suffice." Current forms are published by the Judicial Conference / the federal judiciary's official forms program (uscourts.gov) and in the pamphlet's forms material, not as an Appendix to the Rules.

E. Consequences for the 2014 manual — three separate defects

A 2014 manual's direction to "the Appendix of Forms" was accurate when written and became obsolete on December 1, 2015. The manual now contains three defects, not one:

1. Dead citation target. There is no Appendix of Forms in the rules; a reader following the instruction finds an abrogation parenthetical.
2. Dead safe harbor. Former Rule 84 told parties that use of an Appendix form "suffices." That assurance is gone; a litigant cannot rely on form-compliance as a defense to a pleading or process challenge. The content requirements that the forms illustrated now live in the rule text itself — e.g., the mandatory contents of a summons are set out in Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(a) ("A summons must: ..."), not in a form.
3. Stale numbering. The manual's form numbers reflect the 2007 restyling (Forms 1 through 82, effective December 1, 2007), a numbering scheme that the 2015 abrogation then superseded. Any cross-reference to a numbered Appendix form is doubly out of date.

Replacement guidance for the manual's readers: (a) use the current official forms published by the federal judiciary (uscourts.gov) — e.g., the Summons in a Civil Action (Form AO 440) and the notice/waiver-of-service forms (AO 398/399) [verify current form numbers before publication — § VII, item 3]; (b) check the district's local rules and local forms, which remain a valid source of form requirements under Fed. R. Civ. P. 83; and (c) do not treat any form, current or former, as establishing sufficiency as a matter of law.

[Analysis flag: the interaction between the loss of the Rule 84 safe harbor and federal pleading standards is my reading, not a holding. If the manual discusses pleading sufficiency, pair the annotation with Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007), and Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009), each cited in full and independently verified before publication.]

F. Where the authority is thin or conflicting

- The operative primary source is the Supreme Court's April 29, 2015 order. The materials reviewed supply its citation (575 U.S. 1055) and its effect through the official pamphlet's historical note and the FJC's two publications; the order's own text was not in the file. For a publication-grade annotation, pull the order.
- The 2015 Advisory Committee Note explaining the abrogation (its rationale and any statement about continued availability of forms) was not in the materials reviewed. Do not paraphrase it until obtained.
- The exact title and placement of the current forms material in the official pamphlet is confirmed only at the level of the Foreword's phrase "together with forms"; the forms section itself was not examined. State the point at that level of generality or verify.
- Cornell LII is a reliable index but is secondary; it is used here only to corroborate the parentheticals, which appear identically in the official pamphlet.
- No conflict in the authority reviewed: the pamphlet, the FJC redline, and the FJC transmittal package agree on both the fact of abrogation and the December 1, 2015 effective date.

=====================================================================
V. READY-TO-PASTE ANNOTATION FOR THE MANUAL
=====================================================================

"EDITOR'S NOTE (current through Fed. R. Civ. P. as amended Dec. 1, 2025): The Appendix of Forms no longer exists. The Supreme Court's order of April 29, 2015 (575 U.S. 1055; transmitted to Congress Apr. 29, 2015; H. Doc. 114-33) abrogated both Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms (Forms 1 through 82), effective December 1, 2015. The rules now read: 'Rule 84. [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]' and 'XII. APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]' Any reference in this chapter to a numbered Appendix form, and any reliance on the former Rule 84 statement that the forms 'suffice,' is obsolete. Use the current official forms published by the federal judiciary (uscourts.gov), together with any forms required by the district's local rules under Fed. R. Civ. P. 83. Form numbers cited in the 2014 text reflect the 2007 restyling and are superseded."

=====================================================================
VI. SOURCES, IN FULL
=====================================================================

1. Order of the Supreme Court of the United States, Apr. 29, 2015, 575 U.S. 1055 (2015) (adopting amendments to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure); Cong. Rec., vol. 161, pt. 5, p. 6139, Ex. Comm. 1373; H. Doc. 114-33.
2. Fed. R. Civ. P. 84 (abrogated Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).
3. Fed. R. Civ. P., Title XII, Appendix of Forms (abrogated Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).
4. Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(a), 83, 86.
5. 28 U.S.C. §§ 2072, 2074.

7. Federal Judicial Center, Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure 2015—Civil Rules Redline (Dec. 1, 2015), https://www.fjc.gov/content/309299/amendments-federal-rules-practice-and-procedure-2015-civil-rules-redline.
8. Federal Judicial Center, Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure 2015—Transmittal to Congress (Apr. 29, 2015), https://www.fjc.gov/content/309296/rules-amendments-2015-congress-transmittal.
9. Cornell Legal Information Institute, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (as amended to Dec. 1, 2025), https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp (corroborative only).

=====================================================================

1. Confirm the pre-2015 text of Rule 84 against a 2014 print of the Rules (for the word "suffice").
2. Obtain the text of the April 29, 2015 Supreme Court order (575 U.S. 1055) and the 2015 Advisory Committee Note to the abrogation of Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms; add the Note's rationale if the annotation will explain "why."
