Subject: Term of office of judges of the European Court of Human Rights and eligibility for re-election, in the Convention text presented as amended through Protocol No. 15 — correction of the training slide stating 'renewable six-year terms'.

Jurisdiction / legal order: Council of Europe — European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) system. No other legal order is considered or imported.

=====================================================================
I. SOURCES RELIED ON (cited in full)
=====================================================================

[P1] Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (ETS No. 5), as amended by the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) with effect from its entry into force on 1 August 2021 and of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) with effect from its entry into force on 1 June 2010 — consolidated text published by the European Court of Human Rights / Council of Europe, https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/convention_ENG (text of Article 23 quoted at section II below).

[P2] Protocol No. 15 amending the Convention on the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, CETS No. 213, opened for signature 24 June 2013, entered into force 1 August 2021, Article 2(3) and Article 8 (https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Protocol_15_ENG).

[P3] Explanatory Report to Protocol No. 15, CETS No. 213, paragraphs 10–15 (in particular paragraph 12) (https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_explanatory_report_eng).

[P4] Protocol No. 14 amending the Convention on the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, CETS No. 194, Article 2 (amending Article 23(1) of the Convention), entered into force 1 June 2010. — Cited for the historical step only; see verification flag V-1.

[C1] Council of Europe, Secretariat of the Parliamentary Assembly, Information Note on the election of judges to the European Court of Human Rights, SG-AS (2024) 01 (quoting Article 23(1)–(2) as amended by Protocol No. 15) (https://www.gov.pl/attachment/4cb96533-8779-418e-84e5-c9f09a1885ae). — Corroborative only; not a primary source.

=====================================================================
II. THE GOVERNING TEXT
=====================================================================

[P1], Article 23 ('Terms of office and dismissal'), paragraphs 1–3, in the consolidated text presented as amended through Protocol No. 15:

  '1. The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.
   2. The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration.
   3. No judge may be dismissed from office unless the other judges decide by a majority of two-thirds that that judge has ceased to fulfil the required conditions.'

Composition of that text:

(a) Paragraph 1 was last amended by Protocol No. 14 (in force 1 June 2010) [P4] and was NOT amended by Protocol No. 15. Protocol No. 15 Article 2(3) provides: 'Paragraph 2 of Article 23 of the Convention shall be deleted. Paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 23 of the Convention shall become paragraphs 2 and 3 of Article 23 respectively.' [P2].

(b) The paragraph deleted by Protocol No. 15 was the former age-limit provision: 'The terms of office of judges shall expire when they reach the age of 70.' The Explanatory Report confirms this: 'The age limit applied under Article 23, paragraph 2 of the Convention, as drafted prior to the entry into force of this Protocol, had the effect of preventing certain experienced judges from completing their term of office. It was considered no longer essential to impose an age limit, given the fact that judges' terms of office are no longer renewable.' [P3, para. 12].

(c) Protocol No. 15 inserted a new Article 21(2): 'Candidates shall be less than 65 years of age at the date by which the list of three candidates has been requested by the Parliamentary Assembly, further to Article 22.' [P2, Art. 2(1); P1, Art. 21(2)]. By Article 8(1) of Protocol No. 15 and paragraph 14 of the Explanatory Report, that change applies only to judges elected from lists of candidates submitted after entry into force; judges on lists already submitted (including judges in office and judges-elect on 1 August 2021) remain subject to the pre-existing rule, i.e. expiry of term at age 70 [P3, para. 14].

(d) Article 23(2) as now numbered ('The judges shall hold office until replaced...') is a continuity-of-office rule, not a renewal of the mandate. It permits a judge to continue sitting on cases already under consideration after the term expires and pending replacement; it confers no new term.

=====================================================================
III. ANSWERS
=====================================================================

ASK 2 — Election term.
Nine (9) years. Source: [P1], Article 23(1), first sentence: 'The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years.' Election is by the Parliamentary Assembly under Article 22 [P1]. Corroborated by [C1], which quotes the same sentence and states that 'judges are elected for a fixed term of nine years' and that 'judges are able to serve on the Court until the end of their mandate of 9 years' [C1].

ASK 3 — May a judge be re-elected?
No. Source: [P1], Article 23(1), second sentence: 'They may not be re-elected.' The prohibition is unqualified on the face of the text. Corroborated by [P3, para. 12] ('the fact that judges' terms of office are no longer renewable') and by [C1].

Consequence for the maximum period of judicial service: one nine-year term, subject only to the continuation-in-office rule in Article 23(2) [P1] where a judge whose term has expired continues to deal with cases already under consideration and holds office until replaced. That continuation is not a re-election and does not constitute a second term.

=====================================================================
IV. WHY THE SLIDE IS WRONG — AND WHICH INSTRUMENT CORRECTED IT
=====================================================================

The slide's 'renewable six-year terms' is not a misreading of the current text; it is a statement of a superseded text. The correction is not attributable to Protocol No. 15 (a common misattribution, because Protocol No. 15 is the most recent amendment to Article 23). It is attributable to Protocol No. 14.

Chronology (the pre-2010 step is flagged at V-1):

1. Convention as amended by Protocol No. 11 (in force 1 November 1998) — Article 23(1) provided for election 'for a period of six years' with eligibility for re-election. This is the source of the slide's formulation.
2. Protocol No. 14, CETS No. 194 (in force 1 June 2010) — Article 2 replaced Article 23(1) with the nine-year, non-renewable rule [P4].
3. Protocol No. 15, CETS No. 213 (in force 1 August 2021) — deleted former Article 23(2) (age-70 expiry), renumbered paragraphs 3 and 4 as 2 and 3, and added Article 21(2) (candidates under 65) [P2; P3, paras 11–14]. It did not alter the term of office or the re-election prohibition.

So the slide is approximately 15 years out of date (since 1 June 2010), not 4 years out of date (since 1 August 2021).

=====================================================================
V. WHERE AUTHORITY IS THIN, AND VERIFICATION FLAGS
=====================================================================

V-1 (verification required before publication). The six-year/renewable wording of the Protocol No. 11 era, and the precise article numbering of Protocol No. 11 and Protocol No. 14 Article 2, were not re-fetched in this iteration. The Protocol No. 14 entry-into-force date of 1 June 2010 is confirmed on the face of [P1]. Before the note is published, counsel should confirm against the authentic texts of Protocol No. 11 (CETS No. 155) and Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) the exact pre-2010 wording and the article numbers cited at section IV. Neither answer at section III depends on this: both rest on the current consolidated text [P1].

V-2 (thin authority). The scope of 'They may not be re-elected' is unqualified in the text and bars a further term. Whether it would also bar election for a non-consecutive term after an intervening period is not addressed by any judgment of the Court or by any Committee of Ministers instrument identified in this research; the settled practice is a single nine-year term. The point should not be asserted further than the text supports. It is not material to the slide correction.

V-3 (transitional application). Protocol No. 15 contains no transitional provision for Article 23(1) because Protocol No. 15 did not amend it [P2, Art. 8(4)]. Any question about judges elected before 1 June 2010 whose six-year terms were running at the date of the Protocol No. 14 amendment is a historical question; it does not affect the position under the text as amended through Protocol No. 15. Do not state a transitional rule for Protocol No. 14 Article 2 without checking the authentic text (see V-1).

V-4 (source hierarchy). [C1] is a Council of Europe secretariat document, not primary law. It is cited only as corroboration; the operative citations are [P1] and [P2].

=====================================================================
VI. DRAFT REPLACEMENT SLIDE TEXT (for insertion, subject to review)
=====================================================================

Heading: 'Judges of the European Court of Human Rights — tenure'

- Election term: nine years (ECHR, Article 23(1), first sentence, as amended by Protocol No. 14, in force 1 June 2010).
- Re-election: not permitted — 'They may not be re-elected' (ECHR, Article 23(1), second sentence).
- Election body: Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, from a list of three candidates nominated by the State (ECHR, Article 22).
- Candidate age criterion: candidates must be under 65 at the date the list of three is requested (ECHR, Article 21(2), inserted by Protocol No. 15, in force 1 August 2021; applies only to lists submitted after that date — Protocol No. 15, Article 8(1)).
- Continuation in office: a judge whose term has expired holds office until replaced and continues to deal with cases already under consideration (ECHR, Article 23(2)); this is not a second term.
- Superseded: 'renewable six-year terms' was the position under the Convention as amended by Protocol No. 11 (1998–2010) and has not been correct since 1 June 2010.

=====================================================================
VII. CAVEAT
=====================================================================

This memorandum is a draft prepared for review by a qualified attorney. It is not legal advice and should not be relied on as such. Every statement of law above is tied to the primary source cited at the point at which it is made; where authority is thin or unverified, that is stated at section V rather than resolved.

question: Y137
answer:
# MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

**To:** State-aid team (instructing client)
**From:** Legal researcher
**Re:** Whether Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 can be relied on to exempt aid to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine from notification; and, if not, the instrument the Regulation's scope passage identifies
**Jurisdiction:** European Union — State aid under Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), Council Decision 2010/787/EU, and Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014
**Status:** Research draft. Not legal advice; not for filing with the Commission as it stands.

---

## I. Questions presented

1. Can a State-aid team rely on Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 (the General Block Exemption Regulation, 'GBER') to exempt from the notification requirement of Article 108(3) TFEU aid to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine?
2. If not, which instrument does the Regulation's scope passage identify as dealing with that aid?

## II. Short answers

1. **No.** Aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines is excluded from the GBER's scope outright by Article 1(2)(d) of Regulation 651/2014, and rectical 12 says the Regulation 'should not apply' to it. The block exemption operates only for aid that satisfies 'the conditions laid down in this Article and in Chapter I'; Article 1 is the Chapter I gate. This is a scope exclusion, not a discretionary refusal, so there is no route to exemption by arging compatibility.
2. **Council Decision 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines (OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24).** Both the scope passage (Article 1(2)(d)) and rectical 12 name it.

---

## III. Primary sources relied on (cited in full)

| # | Source | Citation | Provisions used |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 of 17 June 2014 declaring certain categories of aid compatible with the internal market in application of Article 107 and 108 of the Treaty | OJ L 187, 26.6.2014, p. 1 | Art. 1(1), 1(2) intro and (d), 1(2) second subpara., 1(4); Art. 2(13); recital 12; the Chapter I conditioning formula in Arts. 33–35 |
| S2 | Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/1084 of 14 June 2017 amending Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 as regards aid for port and airport infrastructure, notification thresholds for aid for culture and heritage conservation and for aid for sport and multifunctional recreational infrastructures, and regional operating aid schemes for outermost regions, and amending Regulation (EU) No 702/2014 as regards the calculation of eligible costs | OJ (2017) — as consolidated on legislation.gov.uk, footnote F1 to Art. 1 | Amends Art. 1(2)(d) and its footnote (2) |
| S3 | Council Decision 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines | OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24 | Arts. 1, 2, 3, 4 and Annex; Arts. 6, 7, 8; Art. 9 (entry into force, application, expiry) |
| S4 | Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union | Consolidated version | Arts. 107(3), 108(3) (as cross-referenced in S1) |

Text consulted as fetched: EUR-Lex text of S1 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2014.187.01.0001.01.ENG); EUR-Lex text of S3 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dec/2010/787/oj); legislation.gov.uk adopted texts of S1 Art. 1 and body, and the 2017-07-10 revised version of S1 Art. 1; legislation.gov.uk text of S3.

---

## IV. Why the GBER does not exempt this aid

### A. The GBER is an exhaustive, closed list plus a closed list of exclusions

Article 1(1) of S1 provides that the Regulation 'shall apply to the following categories of aid' and then lists them: (a) regional aid; (b) aid to SMEs; (c) aid for environmental protection; (d) R&D&I; (e) training aid; (f) recruitment and employment aid for disadvantaged workers and workers with disabilities; (g) natural-disaster aid; (h) social aid for transport for residents of remote regions; (i) broadband; (j) culture and heritage; (k) sport and multifunctional recreational infrastructure; (l) local infrastructure. Coal-mine closure aid appears nowhere on that list.

Article 1(2) then provides: 'This Regulation shall not apply to:' and includes at point (d) 'aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, as covered by Council Decision No 2010/787' (as adopted in 2014; since S2 the reference reads 'Council Decision 2010/787/EU'). The exclusion is doubly secured: the category is not within Article 1(1), and it is expressly excluded by Article 1(2)(d).

### B. The block exemption is conditioned on Chapter I, of which Article 1 is the first provision

The operative exempting articles in S1 use a uniform formula. By way of illustration, Article 33 provides that aid 'shall be compatible with the internal market within the meaning of Article 107(3) of the Treaty and shall be exempt from the notification requirement of Article 108(3) of the Treaty, provided the conditions laid down in this Article and in Chapter I are fulfilled.' Articles 34 and 35 are worded identically. Article 1 sits in Chapter I. Aid excluded by Article 1(2) therefore can never satisfy 'the conditions laid down ... in Chapter I', and no amount of compliance with an operative article (for example the training or environmental aid articles) cures the defect.

### C. Recital 12 confirms the intent and, importantly, does not leave coal in a gap

Recital 12 of S1: 'This Regulation should not apply to aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, which is dealt with by the Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines. This Regulation should apply to other types of aid in the coal sector, with the exception of regional aid.'

Two consequences follow. First, the exclusion is deliberate and tied to a named alternative instrument, so it is not a drafting omission that could be read down. Second, the GBER is **not** closed to the coal sector as a whole: non-closure aid in the coal sector can still be block-exempted under the relevant Chapter III heading, save for regional aid (rectical 12, final sentence, read with Article 1(2)(e)). The dividing line is therefore functional — is the aid 'to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine'? — not sectoral.

### D. The definition of 'coal' in the GBER is parasitic on the Decision

Article 2(13) of S1: "'coal' means high-grade, medium-grade and low-grade category A and B coal within the meaning of the international codification system for coal established by the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe and clarified in the Council decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines.' The GBER does not run its own coal test; it borrows the Decision's (S3, Article 1(a), worded in materially identical terms). This confirms the two instruments are designed as a single scheme.

### E. The separation-of-activities carve-out does not reach point (d)

The second subparagraph of Article 1(2) of S1 allows an undertak active in excluded sectors to receive GBER aid for its in-scope activities, subject to separation of activities or distinction of costs. But by its own words it applies only 'where an undertak is active in the excluded sectors as referred to in points (a), (b) or (c) of the first subparagraph'. Point (d) — coal-mine closure aid — is not listed. The carve-out therefore cannot be used to bring closure aid back in, and it cannot be used to fund the mine's closure costs through the mine's other activities.

### F. Two independent bars that will often apply on the facts of an uncompetitive mine

Even if a measure escaped Article 1(2)(d), Article 1(4) of S1 provides that the Regulation 'shall not apply to: (a) aid schemes which do not explicitly exclude the payment of individual aid in favour of an undertak which is subject to an outstanding recovery order following a previous Commission decision declaring an aid illegal and incompatible with the internal market ...; (b) ad hoc aid in favour of an undertak as referred to in point (a); (c) aid to undertak in difficulty, with the exception of aid schemes to make good the damage caused by certain natural disasters.' An uncompetitive mine operator is frequently an undertak in difficulty and sometimes carries legacy recovery exposure. Either fact pattern is a second, independent scope bar, and rectical on the point confirms the policy ('Aid granted to undertak in difficulty should be excluded from the scope of this Regulation ... in order to avoid their circumvention').

### G. What the GBER does still reach in this area

Subject to the functional line in C above, the following GBER headings are not excluded merely because the beneficiary is a coal undertak: training aid (Art. 31), recruitment and employment aid for disadvantaged workers and workers with disabilities (Arts. 32–35), environmental investment aid going beyond Union standards (Art. 36 ff.), and, where the conditions fit, energy-efficient district heating and cooling (Art. 46) and energy infrastructure (Art. 48). Whether a given measure is 'aid to facilitate closure' (and so excluded) or genuinely separate aid is the hard question — see section VII.

---

## V. The instrument the scope passage identifies: Decision 2010/787/EU

### A. Status and architecture

S3 is a Council Decision of 10 December 2010. By Article 9 it enters into force on the day following publication, 'shall apply from 1 January 2011', and 'shall expire on 31 December 2027'. Its own recticals describe it as marking 'the transition, for the coal sector, from the application of sector-specific rules to the application of general State aid rules which are applicable to all sectors.'

Article 1 defines: (a) 'coal' — high-grade, medium-grade and low-grade category A and B coal per the UNECE codification; (b) 'closure' — 'the permanent cessation of production and sale of coal'; (c) 'closure plan'; (d) 'coal production unit'; (e) 'coal year'; (f) 'production costs'; (g) 'current production losses'. Article 2(1) states the principle: 'In the context of closure of uncompetitive mines, aid to the coal industry may be considered compatible with the proper functioning of the internal market if it complies with the provisions of this Decision.' Article 2(2) limits aid to coal used for electricity, combined heat and power, coke, and blast-furnace fuelling in the steel industry, where that use takes place in the Union.

### B. Article 3 — closure aid, and the 31 December 2018 gate

Article 3(1) makes aid 'intended specifically to cover the current production losses of coal production units' compatible only if, among other conditions: (a) 'the operation of the coal production units concerned must form part of a closure plan the deadline of which does not extend beyond 31 December 2018'; (b) the units 'must be closed definitively in accordance with the closure plan'; and (c) the aid notified must not exceed the difference between foreseeable production costs and foreseeable revenue for a coal year, with annual correction. Article 3(3) provides that if the units are not closed at the date fixed in the authorised closure plan, 'the Member State concerned shall recover all aid granted in respect of the whole period covered by the closure plan.' The Decision also requires a Member State intending to grant Article 3 closure aid to notify a closure plan for the units concerned to the Commission (paragraph number to be confirmed against the OJ text — the sentence appears in the Article 3 context in the text consulted).

### C. Article 4 — aid to cover exceptional costs

Article 4(1) covers State aid to undertaks which carry out or have carried out a coal-production activity, to enable them to cover costs 'arising from or having arisen from the closure of coal production units and which are not related to current production', up to the amount of such costs, whether incurred by one undertak or several. Article 4(2) refers to the Annex for the closed list of cost categories and states that paragraph 1 'shall not apply to costs resulting from non-compliance with environmental regulations.' The Annex list includes, among others: social welfare benefits from early pensioning-off; other exceptional expenditure on workers who have lost or lose their jobs; pensions and allowances outside the statutory system; readaptation and training costs; free coal or its monetary equivalent; residual costs from coal-specific administrative, legal or tax provisions; additional underground safety work; mining damage caused by the units being closed; duly justified rehabilitation costs of former coal-mining sites; residual costs of former miners' health insurance; cancelling or modification of ongoing contracts (capped at six months of production); exceptional intrinsic depreciation resulting from closure; and surface recultivation.

### D. Supervision provisions

Article 6 (separation of accounts), Article 7 (information to be provided by Member States), Article 8 (implementing measures) complete the scheme. These are the machinery that replaces the GBER's own Chapter I conditions; they are why the Commission can say the aid 'is dealt with by' the Decision.

---

## VI. Decision tree by date of grant (the temporal point counsel must fix before relying on anything)

| Date aid is to be granted | Route | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| On or before 31 Dec 2018, with a closure plan deadline no later than 31 Dec 2018 | Article 3 closure aid possible; notify closure plan to the Commission | S3 Arts. 3(1)(a), 3(3) |
| 1 Jan 2019 – 31 Dec 2027 | Article 3 closure aid for current production losses practically unavailable (the 2018 plan deadline cannot be met); Article 4 aid for Annex exceptional costs remains textually open until the Decision expires | S3 Arts. 3(1)(a), 4, 9 |
| After 31 Dec 2027 | No block exemption (S1 Art. 1(2)(d)) and no sectoral framework (S3 Art. 9 expiry). Notification under Art. 108(3) TFEU and direct assessment under Art. 107(3) TFEU | S1 Art. 1(2)(d); S3 Art. 9; S4 |

In every branch the GBER is unavailable for the closure aid itself. The only variable is which notification route replaces it.

---

## VII. Where authority is thin, conflicting or unverified — read before advising

1. **Hard coal versus lignite.** S3 Art. 1(a) and S1 Art. 2(13) define 'coal' by reference to the UNECE codification, categories A and B. The working reading is that this covers hard coal and excludes brown coal/lignite, which would put a lignite mine outside both instruments — no block exemption and no sectoral framework, hence direct Article 107(3)/108(3). **The UNECE codification itself was not retrieved for this draft.** Confirm before advising on any non-hard-coal site.
2. **Article 4 after 2018.** The 31 Dec 2018 deadline sits in Article 3(1)(a), not in Article 4. Textually, Article 4 aid for residual and exceptional closure costs is not subject to it. Whether the Commission would accept Article 4 aid for a mine that only closes after 2018 is not resolved by the text; pre-notification contact is advisable.
3. **Overlap between Decision Annex items and GBER headings.** Readaptation/training, social welfare benefits and site rehabilitation appear both in the S3 Annex and, in generalized form, under GBER training and environmental aid. Whether a given measure is 'aid to facilitate the closure' (S1 Art. 1(2)(d), excluded) or a genuinely separate in-scope measure is not settled by either text. The risk is that a package split across GBER headings is treated as a single measure; no case law was retrieved for this draft on that point and none is asserted here.
4. **Article 4(2) environmental carve-out.** Rehabilitation costs that remedy non-compliance with environmental regulations are expressly outside Article 4. This is an easy trap in a closure budget and should be screened line by line against the Annex.
5. **GBER period of application.** Article 58 of S1 fixes the Regulation's period of application and that period has been prolonged by amending regulations. The relevant text was not retrieved; the memo therefore makes no assertion about a GBER end date. Confirm the consolidated version in force at the intended grant date, and confirm that Article 1(2)(d) has not been further amended after S2.
6. **Legal basis of S3.** The Decision's preamble (which would show its Treaty basis) was not captured in the passages consulted. Not material to the two answers, but should be cited correctly in any notification.
7. **Citation form.** The 2014 adopted text of Art. 1(2)(d) reads 'Council Decision No 2010/787'; S2 corrected the reference and added the full OJ footnote. Quote the version in force at the relevant date.

---

## VIII. Practical consequence of getting this wrong

Aid that is neither block-exempted nor notified is granted in breach of the standstill obligation in Article 108(3) TFEU (the very obligation the GBER articles dispense with — see the formula in S1 Arts. 33–35). The exposure is a Commission decision declaring the aid illegal and incompatible, with recovery from the beneficiary, plus the Article 3(3) recovery mechanism under the Decision if a closure plan is not honoured. The correct default where scope is doubtful is notification, not reliance on the block exemption.

---

## IX. Verification checklist for counsel

- [ ] Confirm the Member State and the intended grant date; select the branch in section VI.
- [ ] Confirm the coal type against the UNECE codification (item 1).
- [ ] Confirm the consolidated version of S1 in force at the grant date, including whether Art. 1(2)(d) has changed since S2.
- [ ] Screen the closure budget against the S3 Annex, excluding environmental non-compliance costs (item 4).
- [ ] Confirm the paragraph numbering of the closure-plan notification sentence in Art. 3.
- [ ] If any part of the package is proposed under a GBER heading, document the separation of activities and costs and test the 'aid to facilitate closure' boundary (item 3).

---

## X. One-line answers for the file

1. **No** — Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 cannot be relied on; Art. 1(2)(d) excludes the aid from scope, and rectical 12 says the Regulation 'should not apply'.
2. **Council Decision 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines (OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24)** — named by both Art. 1(2)(d) and rectical 12.

The first reads: "Article 46 Investment aid for energy efficient district heating and cooling"

answer:
DRAFT MEMORANDUM FOR REVIEW BY A QUALIFIED ATTORNEY. THIS IS A DRAFT ANALYSIS, NOT LEGAL ADVICE, AND MUST BE CHECKED AGAINST THE CURRENT CONSOLIDATED TREATY TEXT AND HUDOC BEFORE USE.

SUBJECT: Derogability of Article 3, and the Article 2 carve-out in Article 15(2) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

JURISDICTION: Council of Europe. Governing instrument: Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (ETS No. 5), Rome, 4 November 1950, as amended by Protocol No. 11 (ETS No. 155) and Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) ('ECHR' / 'the Convention'). The analysis below states the position for a High Contracting Party to the Convention. It is not assumed to hold for other regional systems: for example, the American Convention on Human Rights (OAS, San Jose, 22 November 1969) contains its own, differently worded non-derogation list in Article 27(2), and nothing here should be read across to it without separate research.

=====================================================================
I. SHORT ANSWER
=====================================================================

1. MAY THE STATE DEROGATE FROM ARTICLE 3 UNDER ARTICLE 15? -- NO.

Article 3 ECHR is expressly non-derogable. Article 15(2) of the Convention provides:

   'No derogation from Article 2, except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war, or from Articles 3, 4 (paragraph 1) and 7 shall be made under this provision.'

Article 3 is named in the enumerated list of provisions from which no derogation may be made. The single exception in that sentence attaches to Article 2, not to Article 3. There is no textual basis on which a Contracting State can derogate from Article 3 in time of war or any other public emergency, and the State's invocation of Article 15(1) cannot reach it.

2. THE NARROW ARTICLE 2 EXCEPTION IN THE SAME CLAUSE: 'DEATHS RESULTING FROM LAWFUL ACTS OF WAR'.

That is the whole of the exception. It is confined to Article 2, it is confined to deaths, and it is confined to deaths resulting from acts of war that are lawful.

=====================================================================
II. QUESTION 1 IN FULL -- ARTICLE 3 IS NON-DEROGABLE
=====================================================================

A. The text.

Article 3 ECHR: 'No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.'

Article 15(1) ECHR confers the power: 'In time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation any High Contracting Party may take measures derogating from its obligations under this Convention to the extent strictly required by the exigencies of the situation, provided that such measures are not inconsistent with its other obligations under international law.'

Article 15(2) removes Article 3 from the scope of that power. The drafting is a single sentence with a single exception, and that exception is grammatically and structurally attached to Article 2 alone ('No derogation from Article 2, except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war, or from Articles 3, 4 (paragraph 1) and 7 ...'). To read the 'lawful acts of war' words as reaching Article 3 would require deleting the words 'from Article 2' and the disjunctive 'or' -- an impermissible reading.

Article 4(1) (prohibition of slavery and servitude) and Article 7 (no punishment without law) are non-derogable on the same footing. Article 15(1)'s power is therefore bounded internally by Article 15(2): the emergency power does not exist at all in respect of the listed provisions.

B. Corroborating authority.

- Ireland v. the United Kingdom, judgment of 18 January 1978, Series A No. 25, para. 163: Article 3 enshrines one of the fundamental values of democratic societies; the Convention prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in absolute terms, irrespective of the victim's conduct.
- Aksoy v. Turkey, judgment of 18 December 1996, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996-VI, para. 62: Article 3 makes no provision for exceptions and no derogation from it is permissible under Article 15(2) even in the event of a public emergency threatening the life of the nation.
- Chahal v. the United Kingdom, judgment of 15 November 1996, Reports 1996-V, para. 79 (Grand Chamber): Article 3 is absolute; the Convention prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment irrespective of the victim's conduct.
- Selmouni v. France [GC], no. 25803/94, para. 95, ECHR 1999-V: the increasingly high standard demanded in the area of protection of human rights requires correspondingly greater firmness in assessing breaches of fundamental values.
- Gafgen v. Germany [GC], no. 22978/05, para. 87, ECHR 2010: Article 3 is absolute and admits of no balancing of the public interest against the individual's ill-treatment, even where the threat is grave (e.g. a kidnapped child).
- Soering v. the United Kingdom, judgment of 7 July 1989, Series A No. 161, para. 88: Article 3 admits of no exceptions or possible justification.
- European Court of Human Rights, Guide on Article 15 of the Convention - Derogation in time of emergency (Council of Europe, last update 31 August 2026), paras. 3, 38-40: Article 15(2) protects Article 2 (except for deaths resulting from lawful acts of war), Article 3, Article 4(1) and Article 7; the effect is that those rights continue to apply in full during any war or public emergency.
- European Court of Human Rights, Factsheet - Derogation in time of emergency (February 2022), section 1: same restatement of Article 15(2).

C. What happens if a State purports to derogate from Article 3 anyway.

(i) The purported derogation is ultra vires and of no legal effect. Article 15(2) is not a procedural formality; it removes the subject matter from the derogation power. A notice under Article 15(3) that names Article 3 does not enlarge the power conferred by Article 15(1).

(ii) Notification cannot cure it. Article 15(3) requires a State 'availing itself of this right of derogation' to keep the Secretary General of the Council of Europe fully informed; there is no 'right of derogation' in respect of Article 3 to which the duty could attach.

(iii) The Court's jurisdiction is unaffected. Applications under Article 34 ECHR alleging torture or inhuman or degrading treatment remain admissible and will be examined on the merits under Article 3; the derogation notice is legally irrelevant to that examination.

(iv) Article 15(1)'s third limb independently bars it. Even if Article 15(2) did not exist, measures must not be 'inconsistent with [the State's] other obligations under international law'. Those obligations include:
   - International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (adopted 16 December 1966, 999 UNTS 171), Article 4(2): no derogation from Articles 6, 7, 8 (paragraphs 1 and 2), 11, 15, 16 and 18.
   - Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (adopted 10 December 1984, 1465 UNTS 85), Article 2(2): 'No exceptional circumstances whatsoever, whether a state of war or a threat of war, internal political instability or any other public emergency, may be invoked as a justification of torture.'
   - Geneva Conventions I-IV of 12 August 1949, common Articles 3 and 147 (grave breaches), and Additional Protocol I of 8 June 1977, Articles 75 and 85(3)(a).
   The Court will examine this limb of its own motion if necessary: Lawless v. Ireland (no. 3), judgment of 1 July 1961, Series A No. 3, para. 40.

(v) The reservation route is closed. A reservation to Article 3 would fall foul of Article 57(1) ECHR (no reservations of a general character) and of the object-and-purpose limit on reservations reflected in Article 19(c) of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (adopted 23 May 1969, 1155 UNTS 331). Article 15 is a derogation clause, not a reservation clause, and cannot be used as one.

(vi) Article 53 ECHR ('Safeguard for existing human rights') prevents any construction of the Convention that would lower protection; a derogation cannot be used to reduce protection below the absolute core.

=====================================================================
III. QUESTION 2 IN FULL -- THE ARTICLE 2 CARVE-OUT
=====================================================================

A. The words.

Article 15(2) ECHR, second element: '... except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war ...'

The exception is narrow on four axes:

(1) It is an exception to the non-derogation rule for Article 2 only. It does not permit derogation from Article 2 generally; outside 'deaths resulting from lawful acts of war', Article 2 remains non-derogable.

(2) It is confined to 'deaths'. It does not authorise derogation in respect of other Article 2 interests (investigation, effective protection by law, procedural safeguards).

(3) It is confined to deaths 'resulting from' the acts -- i.e. a causal link must be shown between the death and an act of war.

(4) It is confined to 'lawful' acts of war. Deaths caused by acts that are unlawful under the law of armed conflict are not covered and remain fully within Article 2, with no derogation available. The qualifier 'lawful' does the substantive work: the carve-out tracks international humanitarian law, not the State's own say-so.

B. Interaction with Article 2's internal limitation.

Article 2(2) ECHR contains a separate, internal limitation (use of force no more than absolutely necessary in defence from unlawful violence, to effect a lawful arrest or prevent escape, or in action lawfully taken to quell a riot or insurrection). That is not a derogation; it operates within Article 2 in normal times. The Article 15(2) carve-out is a different mechanism operating in war. The two should not be conflated in any pleading or notice: the first is an element of the right, the second is an exception to the non-derogation rule. Article 3 has neither.

C. Interaction with Protocols Nos. 6, 7 and 13.

- Protocol No. 6 (ETS No. 9), Article 1 abolishes the death penalty; Article 2 permits a State to make provision in its law for the death penalty in respect of acts committed in time of war or imminent threat of war; Article 3 provides: 'No derogation from the provisions of this Protocol shall be made under Article 15 of the Convention.' Article 4 prohibits reservations.
- Protocol No. 13 (CETS No. 187), Article 1 abolishes the death penalty in all circumstances; Article 2 provides: 'No derogation from the provisions of this Protocol shall be made under Article 15 of the Convention.'
- Protocol No. 7 (ETS No. 117), Article 4(3): 'No derogation from this Article shall be made under Article 15 of the Convention.' (ne bis in idem).
- The Court's Guide on Article 15 (para. 39) lists these three Protocols as containing the corresponding non-derogation clauses.

Practical consequence: for a State party to Protocol No. 13, the Article 15(2) carve-out cannot be used to justify a death penalty in wartime, because Protocol No. 13 abolishes the penalty in all circumstances and itself prohibits derogation. For a State party to Protocol No. 6 only, the wartime death-penalty permission in Article 2 of that Protocol operates as a substantive rule, not as an Article 15 derogation.

D. Where the authority is thin or contested (flagged for the reviewing attorney).

- No judgment of the Court located in the research set gives an authoritative construction of the phrase 'lawful acts of war' in Article 15(2). The content must be derived from international humanitarian law (Geneva Conventions I-IV of 12 August 1949; Additional Protocol I of 8 June 1977, in particular the principles of distinction and proportionality at Articles 48, 51 and 52). Any opinion relying on this carve-out should say so expressly rather than assert a settled meaning.
- The travaux preparatoires are cited in the source set (Council of Europe, document CDH(77)5, collected travaux on Article 15) but their content was not verified for this draft; if the point matters, the travaux should be read directly before relying on them.
- There is a genuine doctrinal dispute, which this draft does not resolve, whether the carve-out is properly a power of derogation at all or a declaratory recognition that deaths caused by lawful acts of belligerency were never within the intended reach of Article 2. The text places it inside Article 15(2) as an exception to non-derogation, and this draft follows the text; but the point is arguable and should be researched before it is litigated.
- The research set contains no authority applying Article 15(2) to a live interstate armed conflict on the scale of a modern war; the Court's Article 15 case law is dominated by internal emergencies (Lawless; Brannigan and McBride; Aksoy; Bas).

=====================================================================
IV. ARTICLE 15(1) AND 15(3) -- COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST (SECONDARY TO THE ASKS)
=====================================================================

Article 15(1) conditions (all must hold even for derogable articles):
- 'time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation' -- Lawless v. Ireland (no. 3), 1 July 1961, Series A No. 3, para. 28 (an exceptional situation of crisis or emergency affecting the whole population and constituting a threat to the organised life of the community).

Article 15(3) procedure:
- Notification to the Secretary General of the Council of Europe, with the measures taken and the reasons for them; further notification when measures cease.
- An official and public notice of derogation is a precondition to reliance on Article 15: Cyprus v. Turkey, no. 8007/77, Report of the European Commission of Human Rights of 4 October 1983, paras. 66-68; Rainbow Mission Foundation and Others v. Hungary, 2026, para. 113 (as cited in the Court's Guide on Article 15).

DELIVERABLE: MODEL ARBITRATION TEXT AND SOURCE ANSWER. Draft prepared for review by a qualified attorney. Not legal advice. The text is jurisdiction-neutral by design because the request names no seat and no enforcement State; it therefore carries a mandatory seat/enforcement-State election and a variance checklist (Part F), and no State-specific rule is assumed to hold in any other State.

=====================================================================
PART 0 - ANSWER TO ASK 2: WHICH UNCITRAL TEXT TO RETRIEVE
=====================================================================

RETRIEVE: the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (1985), with amendments as adopted in 2006.

Grounds, verbatim from the source: 'The Model Law is designed to assist States in reforming and modernizing their laws on arbitral procedure so as to take into account the particular features and needs of international commercial arbitration. It covers all stages of the arbitral process from the arbitration agreement, the composition and jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal and the extent of court intervention through to the recognition and enforcement of the arbitral award.' - UNCITRAL, Model Law page, https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/modellaw/commercial_arbitration (fetched 2026-11-23T04:47:28Z, sha256 2b767ee0758e).

That single sentence names all four topics the team's model text must cover. No other UNCITRAL text in the material does. Mapping of requested element to instrument:

  (a) Arbitration agreement: Model Law art. 7 (as amended 2006) and art. 8; New York Convention art. II.
  (b) Tribunal composition and jurisdiction: Model Law arts. 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16.
  (c) Court intervention: Model Law arts. 5, 6, 8, 9, 13(3), 16(3), 17J, 27, 34.
  (d) Recognition and enforcement of the award: Model Law arts. 35 and 36; New York Convention arts. III, IV, V, and VII(1).

Why the other candidate texts are not the answer:

  - UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules. These are procedural rules that parties adopt by agreement. The Rules page describes them as covering 'appointment of arbitrators and the conduct of arbitral proceedings, and establishing rules in relation to the form, effect and interpretation of the award' (https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/contractualtexts/arbitration, sha256 81f0ae56c81c). They do not regulate the extent of court intervention and they do not regulate recognition and enforcement of the award; those are legislative and treaty matters. The Rules page contains no reference to the Model Law at all: the harness searched the full 12,741-character text of that page and none of 'UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration', 'Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration', 'UNCITRAL Model Law', 'Model Law', '1985 Model Law' appears. That absence is consistent with the division of subject matter and does not make ask 2 unanswerable, because the answer is stated on the Model Law page in the same source set. The Rules are still retrieved, but as the drafting layer, not as the answer.
  - New York Convention (New York, 1958). Treaty on enforcement only. The UNCITRAL arbitration index page states: 'Under the New York Convention, States undertake to give effect to an agreement to arbitrate, and to recognize and enforce awards made in other States.' It is retrieved as a companion text, not as the model text.
  - UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Conciliation (the 03-90953 PDF in the source set, sha256 5e22fe5b2aa4). A different UNCITRAL text dealing with conciliation, not arbitration. Not used for any statement in this draft.
  - UNCITRAL Rules on Transparency in Treaty-based Investor-State Arbitration (2014) and the Mauritius Convention on Transparency (2014). Treaty-based investor-State only; outside scope on the assumptions stated in Part F(7).

Retrieve alongside the Model Law: (i) the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules in the 2021 version (incorporating art. 1(5) and the Expedited Rules appendix) for the procedural and clause layer; (ii) the New York Convention for the enforcement layer; (iii) the UNCITRAL Secretariat Guide on the New York Convention (2016) for article-level commentary.

=====================================================================
PART A - THE ARBITRATION AGREEMENT
=====================================================================

A1. Agreement to arbitrate. 'Any dispute, controversy or claim arising out of or relating to this Agreement, including any question as to its existence, validity, interpretation, performance, breach or termination, the consequences of its nullity, and any non-contractual claim arising out of or in connection with it, shall be referred to and finally resolved by arbitration.'

A2. Rules and administration. 'The arbitration shall be [administered by [institution] under] the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules [as revised in 2010 and as adopted in 2021, including, where the parties have expressly so agreed in writing, the UNCITRAL Expedited Arbitration Rules in the Appendix], as modified by this Part A and Part B.' Drafting note: the expedited opt-in must be express. The Rules page states: 'The phrase where the parties so agree in that paragraph emphasizes the need for the parties express consent for the Expedited Rules to apply to the arbitration.' Do not bury the opt-in in a schedule.

A3. Form of the agreement. Insert the option that matches the seat State's enactment:
  Option I (Model Law art. 7 as amended 2006, written-form option): 'This arbitration agreement is concluded in writing. It may be concluded, evidenced or recorded by electronic means, and reference in this Agreement to any document containing an arbitration clause constitutes an arbitration agreement in writing, provided that the reference makes that clause part of the contract.'
  Option II (Model Law art. 7 as amended 2006, no form requirement): 'This arbitration agreement may be concluded in any form; no written form is required.'
  Justification: the 2006 revision 'is intended to modernise the form required of an arbitration agreement to better conform with international contract practices' (Model Law page).

A4. Separability. 'The arbitration agreement in this Part A is separable from the rest of this Agreement. A decision by the tribunal that the Agreement is null and void shall not entail ipso jure the invalidity of the arbitration agreement.' (Model Law art. 16(1).)

A5. Governing law of the arbitration agreement (express designation). 'This arbitration agreement, and any question as to its existence, validity or scope, shall be governed by the law of [seat State].' Drafting note: the Model Law does not state which law governs the arbitration agreement, and national approaches diverge. Express designation does not remove the conflict but materially reduces it. See Part H3.

A6. Carve-out for court relief (optional). 'Nothing in this Part A prevents a party from applying to a court for [interim or conservatory relief] [preservation of evidence] before or during the arbitration, and any such application is not a waiver of this agreement and is not inconsistent with it.' (Model Law arts. 9 and 17J.)

=====================================================================
PART B - TRIBUNAL COMPOSITION AND JURISDICTION
=====================================================================

B1. Number of arbitrators. 'The tribunal shall consist of [one] [three] arbitrator(s).' Default if the clause is silent: three arbitrators (Model Law art. 10(2)).

B2. Appointment. 'The [claimant shall appoint one arbitrator in the notice of arbitration] [each party shall appoint one arbitrator within [30] days of the notice of arbitration]. The [two party-appointed arbitrators shall appoint the presiding arbitrator] [the presiding arbitrator shall be appointed by [appointing authority]] within [30] days of the appointment of the second arbitrator. If any appointment is not made within the applicable period, [the appointing authority] shall make the appointment on the request of any party.' (Model Law arts. 11(2), 11(3), 11(4).)

B3. Multi-party appointment. 'Where there are more than two parties and the dispute is referred to three arbitrators, the [claimants jointly] [respondents jointly] shall each appoint one arbitrator. Failing agreement on the designation of the appointing authority within [30] days, [the appointing authority] shall be [designated by [institution]] [designated by the Secretary-General of the Permanent Court of Arbitration].' (Model Law art. 11(4).)

B4. Independence, impartiality, disclosure. 'Each arbitrator shall be and remain independent and impartial and shall disclose without delay any circumstances likely to give rise to justifiable doubts as to independence or impartiality. A party may challenge an arbitrator it has appointed, or in whose appointment it participated, only for reasons of which it becomes aware after the appointment has been made.' (Model Law arts. 12(1), 12(2).)

B5. Challenge procedure. 'A party challenging an arbitrator shall state the reasons within [15] days of becoming aware of the constitution of the tribunal or of the circumstances referred to in article 12(2). Unless the challenged arbitrator withdraws or the other party agrees, the tribunal, or failing that [the appointing authority], shall decide on the challenge. If the challenge is rejected, the challenging party may apply to [the court designated under article 6] within [30] days to decide the challenge; that decision is not subject to appeal.' (Model Law art. 13(2), 13(3).)

B6. Competence-competence and jurisdictional objections. 'The tribunal has power to rule on its own jurisdiction, including any objection with respect to the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement. A plea that the tribunal does not have jurisdiction shall be raised not later than the submission of the statement of defence; a plea that the tribunal is exceeding the scope of its authority shall be raised as soon as the matter alleged to be beyond the scope of its authority is raised during the arbitral proceedings. The tribunal may admit a later plea if it considers the delay justified. The tribunal may rule on a plea either as a preliminary question or in an award on the merits.' (Model Law art. 16(1), 16(2), 16(3).)

B7. Interim measures by the tribunal. 'The tribunal may, at the request of a party, grant interim measures and preliminary orders in accordance with Chapter IV A of the Model Law as enacted in [seat State].' Version note: Chapter IV A replaced art. 17 on 7 July 2006 (Model Law page: 'a new chapter IV A to replace article 17'). If the seat State enacted the 1985 text, the tribunal's power is the narrower art. 17 (1985) and the clause must be redrafted. See Part F(1).

B8. Seat, language, applicable law. 'The seat of the arbitration shall be [city, State]. The tribunal may hold hearings, meetings and deliberations at any convenient place; the award is made at the seat. The language of the arbitration shall be [English]. The tribunal shall apply the law of [State] to the substance of the dispute; the law of the seat governs the arbitration procedure.' (Model Law arts. 20, 22, 28(1), 28(2).)

=====================================================================
PART C - COURT INTERVENTION
=====================================================================

C1. Extent of intervention. 'In matters governed by the law of [seat State] on international commercial arbitration, no court shall intervene except where so provided in that law.' (Model Law art. 5.)

C2. Designated court. 'The functions referred to in articles 11(3), 11(4), 13(3), 14, 16(3), 17J, 27, 34, 35 and 36 shall be performed by [the designated court or courts of [seat State]].' (Model Law art. 6.) The clause must name the court or point precisely to the statutory designation; a generic reference to 'the competent court' invites a jurisdictional fight at the worst moment.

C3. Referral to arbitration by a court. 'A court before which an action is brought in a matter which is the subject of this arbitration agreement shall, if a party so requests not later than when submitting its first statement on the substance of the dispute, refer the parties to arbitration, unless it finds that the agreement is null and void, inoperative or incapable of being performed.' (Model Law art. 8(1).)

C4. Interim measures from a court. 'It is not incompatible with this arbitration agreement for a party to request, before or during arbitral proceedings, from a court an interim measure of protection, and for a court to grant such a measure.' (Model Law art. 9; see also art. 17J.)

C5. Court assistance in taking evidence. 'The tribunal, or a party with the approval of the tribunal, may request the competent court of [seat State] to assist in taking evidence.' (Model Law art. 27.)

C6. Setting aside: exclusive recourse. 'Recourse to a court against an arbitral award may be made only by an application for setting aside in accordance with article 34 of the Model Law as enacted in [seat State]. The grounds are limited to those listed in article 34(2): incapacity of a party or invalidity of the arbitration agreement; lack of proper notice or inability to present one's case; the award dealing with matters beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration; composition of the tribunal or arbitral procedure not in accordance with the agreement or the law of the seat; non-arbitrability of the subject matter; conflict with the public policy of the seat State. The application must be made within three months of receipt of the award or, where a request for correction or an additional award has been made, of the disposal of that request.' (Model Law art. 34(1), 34(2), 34(3).)

C7. Waiver of objections. 'A party who knows that a provision of the law of [seat State] from which the parties may derogate, or a requirement under this arbitration agreement, has not been complied with and yet proceeds with the arbitration without stating its objection without undue delay, waives its right to object.' (Model Law art. 4.)

=====================================================================
PART D - RECOGNITION AND ENFORCEMENT OF THE AWARD
=====================================================================

D1. Finality. 'The award shall be final and binding on the parties. The parties undertake to carry out the award without delay.' (Model Law art. 35(1); UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules art. 34.) See Part H4 on the limits of any waiver of recourse.

D2. Enforcement in the seat State. 'An arbitral award, irrespective of the State in which it was made, shall be recognised as binding and, upon application in writing to the competent court of [seat State], shall be enforced, subject only to the grounds for refusal set out in article 36.' (Model Law art. 35(1), 36.)

D3. Documents for enforcement. 'The party relying on an award or applying for its enforcement shall supply the duly authenticated original award or a duly certified copy of it, and the original arbitration agreement or a duly certified copy of it. If the award or the agreement is not in [the official language of the court], the party shall supply a translation into that language.' (Model Law art. 35(2) as amended in 2006, which refers to the documentary requirements of article IV of the New York Convention.)

D4. Cross-border enforcement. Clause: 'The parties intend that any award rendered in the arbitration be enforceable as a foreign arbitral award under the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (New York, 10 June 1958) in any Contracting State.' Enforcement checklist tied to the Convention:
  - art. I(1): the Convention applies to awards made in the territory of a State other than the State where recognition and enforcement are sought, and to awards not considered domestic in the enforcement State. Choose the seat with the target enforcement States in mind.
  - art. I(3): the two reservations a Contracting State may make, reciprocity and commercial. Check each enforcement State's status and reservations.
  - art. II: each Contracting State shall recognise an agreement in writing under which the parties undertake to submit to arbitration, and its court, when seized of an action in a matter covered by such an agreement, shall at the request of one of the parties refer them to arbitration. UNCITRAL index page: 'Under the New York Convention, States undertake to give effect to an agreement to arbitrate, and to recognize and enforce awards made in other States.'
  - art. III: Contracting States shall recognise awards as binding and enforce them in accordance with the rules of procedure of the territory where the award is relied upon, under conditions no more onerous than those imposed on domestic awards.
  - art. IV: the documentary conditions for enforcement (authenticated award, agreement, translation).
  - art. V(1) and V(2): the exhaustive grounds on which recognition and enforcement may be refused.
  - art. V(1)(e): refusal where the award has been set aside or suspended by a competent authority of the country in which, or under the law of which, that award was made. This is why the choice of seat in Part B8 and the setting-aside exposure in Part C6 must be assessed together.
  - art. VII(1): the more-favourable-right provision; a party may rely on a more favourable enforcement regime under the law of the enforcement State. See the Recommendation regarding the interpretation of articles II(2) and VII(1) (2006) and the UNCITRAL Secretariat Guide on the New York Convention (2016).

D5. Interest and costs. '[The tribunal may award simple or compound interest on any sum awarded, from such date and at such rate as it determines. The tribunal shall fix the costs of the arbitration in accordance with article 30 of the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules.]' Drafting note: the enforceability of interest components raises public-policy questions in some enforcement States; verify per State.

=====================================================================
PART E - OPTIONAL MODULES (insert only on instruction)
=====================================================================

E1. Expedited procedure: express opt-in under art. 1(5) of the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules as adopted in 2021, incorporating the UNCITRAL Expedited Arbitration Rules in the Appendix. Express consent is required (Rules page, quoted at A2).
E2. Joinder and consolidation: the Model Law does not regulate either; they must come from institutional rules or an express clause.
E3. Confidentiality: the Model Law does not provide for it; use an express clause (see the UNCITRAL Model Clause on Confidentiality listed on the arbitration index page).
E4. Multiple contracts in a single arbitration; single-claimant/multi-respondent mechanics.
E5. Sovereign immunity waiver: only if a party is a State or State entity, and only with separate advice.

=====================================================================
PART F - JURISDICTION AND VARIANCE CHECKLIST (MANDATORY BEFORE USE)
=====================================================================

The model text is not self-executing. The Model Law is a template for legislation; it binds only as enacted by the seat State, and its content differs between enactments. Before the text is used, confirm the following for the named seat State and for each anticipated enforcement State:

F1. Version enacted: 1985 original or 2006 amended. Model Law page: 'As of 2006, the standard version of the Model Law is the amended version. The original 1985 text is also reproduced in view of the many national enactments based on this original version.' Consequences of the 1985 text: different art. 7 form requirement; art. 17 (1985) instead of Chapter IV A for interim measures; unamended art. 35(2) documentary requirements; no art. 2A interpretive rule.
F2. Declarations, reservations and non-uniform enactments made by the seat State on adoption.
F3. Identity of the court designated under art. 6, to be inserted at C2.
F4. Whether an exclusion or waiver of the setting-aside remedy is permitted at the seat. In most enactments art. 34 is not derogable.
F5. For each enforcement State: New York Convention Contracting State status, reciprocity and commercial reservations under art. I(3), and the local procedural rules that apply under art. III.
F6. Whether the dispute is international and commercial within Model Law art. 1(1), 1(3) and the footnote recommending a wide interpretation of 'commercial'. The Model Law applies only to international commercial arbitration.
F7. Whether any party is a State or State entity and the claim is treaty-based: if so, the UNCITRAL Rules on Transparency (2014) and the Mauritius Convention on Transparency (2014) may apply. This draft assumes they do not.
F8. Whether the arbitration would be domestic in the seat State; if so, the Model Law does not apply to it.

=====================================================================
PART G - SOURCE REGISTER (FULL CITATIONS)
=====================================================================

G1. UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration, adopted by the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law on 21 June 1985 (General Assembly resolution 40/72 of 11 December 1985), with amendments as adopted by UNCITRAL on 7 July 2006 (General Assembly resolution 61/33 of 4 December 2006). UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules, adopted 28 April 1976; as revised in 2010 (General Assembly resolution 65/22 of 6 December 2010); with article 1(4) as adopted in 2013 (General Assembly resolution 68/109 of 16 December 2013) and article 1(5) as adopted in 2021 (General Assembly resolution 76/108 of 9 December 2021). https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/contractualtexts/arbitration.

G7. UNCITRAL Rules on Transparency in Treaty-based Investor-State Arbitration (effective 1 April 2014); United Nations Convention on Transparency in Treaty-based Investor-State Arbitration (New York, 2014) ('Mauritius Convention on Transparency'). Not applicable on the assumptions in F7.

=====================================================================
